text: 1.1. Not long afterward Chosroes, learning that Belisarius had begun to win Italy too for the Emperor Justinian, was no longer able to restrain his mind, but wished to devise pretexts by which he might break the treaty under some specious word.
1.2. Consulting about these things with Alamoundaras, he bade him provide causes of war.

1.3. And he, charging Arethas that he was using violence against him over the boundaries of the land, came to blows with him in time of peace, and on this pretext began to overrun the land of the Romans.
1.4. And he declared that he himself was not breaking the treaty of the Persians and Romans, since neither party had enrolled him in it.
1.5. And this was so. For no account had ever been made of the Saracens in the treaties, since they are comprehended under the name of the Persians and the Romans.

1.6. This country, which then was disputed by the Saracens of both sides, is called Strata, and is turned toward the south wind of the city of Palmyra, bearing neither tree nor any of the good things of the cornfields (for it is exceedingly burnt by the sun), but set apart from of old for the pasturing of certain flocks.

1.7. Arethas, then, insisted that the place was the Romans', inferring it from the name, which it chanced to have from of old among all (for Strata means the paved road in the Latin tongue), and using the testimonies of most ancient men.
1.8. But Alamoundaras by no means thought fit to contend over the name, but said that the owners of the flocks had from of old paid him rent for the pasture there.

1.9. Therefore the Emperor Justinian entrusted the arbitration of the disputed points to Strategius, a patrician and commander of the royal treasuries, and otherwise intelligent and well-born, and besides to Summus, who had been commander of the soldiers in Palestine.
1.10. This Summus was the brother of Julian, who a little before had gone on an embassy to the Ethiopians and the Homerites.

1.11. And of these two, the one, Summus, thought fit that the Romans should not abandon the country, while Strategius begged the emperor not, for the sake of a country small and of no account at all, but barren and altogether fruitless, to grant to the Persians, who desired war, pretexts for the war. The Emperor Justinian, then, took counsel about these things, and much time was spent on this arbitration.

1.12. But Chosroes, the King of the Persians, declared that the treaty had been broken by Justinian, who had lately displayed a great plot against his house, in that he had attempted to make Alamoundaras his ally in time of peace.

1.13. For he said that Summus, lately coming to him ostensibly for the arbitration, had got round him by promises of great sums of money, on condition that he should go over to the Romans, and he produced letters which the Emperor Justinian had written to Alamoundaras about these things.

1.14. And he insisted that he had also sent a letter to some of the Huns, urging them to invade the land of the Persians and ravage the places there as much as possible. This letter he said the Huns themselves had handed to him, coming into his presence.
1.15. These were the charges Chosroes brought against the Romans, purposing to break the treaty. Whether, however, in saying these things he chanced to be telling the truth, I cannot say.

2.1. Meanwhile Vittigis, the leader of the Goths, already worn down by the war, sent two envoys to him to persuade him to make an expedition against the Romans—not Goths, however, lest by being recognized at once they should confound what was being done, but Ligurian priests, led to this deed by ample sums of money.
2.2. Of these the one who seemed the worthier was set in the embassy, clothed with the appearance and name of a bishop, though it in no way belonged to him; and the other followed serving him.

2.3. And going by the road to the regions of Thrace, they made companion of a man from there who should be for them an interpreter of the Syrian and the Greek tongue, and escaping the notice of all the Romans they reached the country of the Persians. For, being established in time of peace, the Romans did not keep guard there exactly.

2.4. And coming into the presence of Chosroes they spoke as follows: "All other envoys, O King, for the most part chance to be set in the embassy for their own advantage, but us Vittigis, King of the Goths and the Italians, has sent to make the case on behalf of your empire; and consider that he himself, present, now speaks these things to you.
2.5. If anyone, O King, summing it up, should say that you have given over both your kingship and all men to Justinian, he would speak rightly.

2.6. For he, being by nature a lover of innovation and enamoured of what in no way belongs to him, and unable to remain within the established order, has desired to seize all the earth, and has been eager to encompass every realm.

2.7. Then (for he was not able to attack the Persians alone, nor, while the Persians opposed him, was he able to go against others) he resolved to deceive you with the veil of peace, and by forcing the rest to make great powers his allies against your empire.

2.8. Having already destroyed the kingdom of the Vandals and subdued the Moors, the Goths standing out of his way under the name of friendship, he comes against us with great sums of money and many men.

2.9. And it is clear that, if he should be able to destroy the Goths altogether, he will make an expedition against the Persians together with us and those already enslaved, neither having in mind the name of friendship nor blushing at any of his oaths.

2.10. While, then, some hope of safety is still left you, do us no further harm, nor suffer it yourself, but look in our evils at what a little later will befall the Persians, and consider that the Romans would never be well-disposed toward your kingship, but, becoming superior in power, will not delay to display their hatred toward the Persians.

2.11. Use, then, your power in season; do not seek it when it has ceased. For the height of opportunities, when relaxed, is by no means wont to return. And it is better, having anticipated, to be in safety, than, having come too late for the opportunities, to suffer the most shameful of all things at the hands of the enemy."

2.12. When Chosroes heard this, it seemed to him that Vittigis advised him well, and he was still more eager to break the treaty. For, held by envy toward the Emperor Justinian, he by no means resolved to reckon that these words came to him from men most hostile to the Emperor Justinian.
2.13. But by his wishing it, he came of his own accord to be persuaded. Which indeed he did a little later in the case of the arguments of the Armenians and the Lazi, as shall presently be told.
2.14. And yet they brought such charges against Justinian as might fitly be praises for a noble king: that he was eager to make his own kingship greater and far more illustrious.

2.15. For these things one might bring also against Cyrus the King of the Persians and Alexander the Macedonian. But justice is by no means wont to dwell with envy. For these reasons Chosroes purposed to break the treaty.

3.1. Meanwhile another thing befell, of the following kind. That Symeon, who had given over the Pharangium to the Romans, persuaded the Emperor Justinian, while the war was still at its height, to gift him with certain villages of Armenian men.
3.2. And having become master of the places, he was killed by a plot at the hands of those who had owned them of old.

3.3. The evil being accomplished, the perpetrators of the murder fled to the country of the Persians. They were two brothers, sons of Perozes. And the emperor, hearing this, gives the villages to Amazaspes, the nephew of Symeon, and set him up as commander over the Armenians.

3.4. This Amazaspes, as time went on, one of his intimates, Acacius by name, slandered to the Emperor Justinian, saying that he was doing mischief to the Armenians and wished to hand over to the Persians both Theodosiopolis and certain other towns.
3.5. Having said this, Acacius, by the emperor's purpose, killed Amazaspes by treachery, and held the command of Armenia himself, the emperor having given it.
3.6. Being wicked by nature, he had whereby he might display the dispositions of his soul. He became, then, the most savage of all men toward his subjects.

3.7. For he plundered their money with no account, and appointed for them a payment of tribute, never before existing, of four centenaria. And the Armenians (for they were no longer able to bear him), taking counsel together, killed Acacius and fled to the Pharangium.
3.8. Therefore the emperor sent Sittas against them from Byzantium. For Sittas was passing his time there, since the treaty with the Persians had been made for the Romans.

3.9. And he, coming to the Armenians, at first went slowly into the war, but hastened to tame them and to set the men back into their former dispositions, promising to persuade the emperor to remit to them the new payment of tribute.
3.10. But when the emperor reproached him much for his delay and reviled him, led by the slanders of Adolius the son of Acacius, then at last Sittas prepared the matters concerning the engagement.
3.11. First, then, by promises of many good things he attempted to persuade and win over some of them, that the mastery over the rest might become for him easier and less toilsome.
3.12. And the race of those called the Aspetiani, being great and populous,

3.13. wished to go over to him. And sending to Sittas in writing, they begged him to give them pledges that, if, in the engagement, abandoning their kinsmen, they should come into the Roman battle-line, they would remain altogether unharmed, holding their own.
3.14. And he, gladly writing in a little book the pledges as they asked, gave them, and having sealed the writing sent it to them.
3.15. Taking courage that through them he would master the war without battle, he went with his whole army to a place called Oenochalakon, where it chanced that the Armenians were encamped.
3.16. But by some chance those who had the book, going by another road, were by no means able to meet the Aspetiani.
3.17. A portion, however, of the Roman army, meeting a few of them and not knowing the agreement, treated them as enemies.

3.18. And Sittas himself, taking their children and women somewhere in a cave, killed them, either not understanding what had happened or holding the Aspetiani in anger because they did not come over to him as had been agreed.

3.19. And they, now held by anger, drew themselves up for battle together with all the rest. But since both sides were in difficult and precipitous ground, they did not fight in one place, but scattered among the foothills and glens. It chanced, then, that a few of the Armenians and Sittas, having not many followers, came very near one another, a glen being between them.

3.20. And both were horsemen. Sittas, then, with a few following him, crossing the glen against his adversaries, drove on, but the Armenians, withdrawing back, stood; and Sittas no longer pursued, but remained where he was.

3.21. And suddenly one of the Roman army, a Herul by race, who had made a pursuit against the enemy and was riding back from there in anger, came to those under Sittas. And it chanced that Sittas had planted his spear in the ground; this the horse of the Herul, falling upon it with much force, broke.

3.22. This grieved the general exceedingly, and one of the Armenians, seeing him, recognized him and insisted to all the rest that this was Sittas. For it happened that he had no helmet on his head. Therefore he did not escape the notice of the enemy, that he had come there with a few men.
3.23. Sittas, then, when he heard the Armenian saying this, and his spear, as has been said, broken off lay on the ground, drawing his sword, at once attempted to cross the glen.

3.24. But the enemy with much haste drove against him, and one, overtaking him in the glen, struck him on the top of the head with his sword, a crosswise blow. And he took off the whole crown of the head,

3.25. but the iron in no way touched the bone. And Sittas drove on still more than before; but Artabanes, the son of John, an Arsacid, falling upon him from behind and striking him with his spear, killed him.

3.26. And thus Sittas vanished from among men in no account, unworthily of his valour and of his deeds ever done against the enemy, a man exceedingly fair in body and valiant in war, and the best general of his time, second to none.
3.27. But some say that Sittas perished not at the hands of Artabanes, but that Solomon, a very obscure man among the Armenians, made away with the man.

3.28. On the death of Sittas the emperor bade Bouzes go against the Armenians; and he, when he came very near, sent to them, promising to reconcile all the Armenians to the emperor and asking some of the men of repute to come to a parley with him about these things.

3.29. The rest, then, could neither trust Bouzes nor were willing to accept his words. But there was a man most friendly to him, an Arsacid, John by name, the father of Artabanes, who then, trusting Bouzes as a friend, came to him together with Bassaces his son-in-law and a few others; and these, when they had come to a place and bivouacked where they were to meet Bouzes on the morrow, perceived that they had come into an encircling by the Roman army.

3.30. Bassaces, then, the son-in-law, much entreated John to take to flight. But when he could not persuade him, leaving him alone there, together with all the rest, escaping the notice of the Romans, he rode back again by the same road.

3.31. And Bouzes, finding John alone, killed him; and from this the Armenians, having no longer any hope toward the Romans concerning an agreement, nor being able to overcome the emperor in war, came to the King of the Persians, Bassaces leading them, an energetic man.

3.32. Of these the foremost, then coming into the presence of Chosroes, spoke as follows: "There are many of us Arsacids, O master, descendants of that Arsaces who chanced to be no stranger to the kingship of the Parthians, when the affairs of the Persians lay under the Parthians, and who became an illustrious king, second to none of his time.
3.33. We are now present before you, all having become slaves and fugitives, not willingly, however, but constrained as much as possible, in appearance by the Roman power, but in true word by your

3.34. judgement, O King; if indeed he who gives strength to those who wish to do wrong might justly bear also the blame of the deeds. And it shall be told a little further back, so that you may be able to follow all that has been done.

3.35. For Arsaces, the last king of our ancestors, ceded his rule of his own free will to Theodosius the Emperor of the Romans, on condition that all those who by descent should belong to him for all time should both live otherwise in freedom and never be subject to tribute.
3.36. And we preserved the agreement until you made these famous treaties, which, calling them a common ruin, one would not, we think, err.
3.37. For thenceforth, taking no thought of friends and enemies, your friend in word, O King, but in deed your foe, confounded and threw into confusion all human affairs.

3.38. Which you yourself also will not long after know, as soon as he is able to subdue the men of the West altogether. For what of the things forbidden before did he not do? Or what of the things well established did he not disturb?

3.39. Did he not appoint for us a payment of tribute not before existing, and enslave the Tzani, who were our neighbours and independent, and set a Roman commander over the king of the wretched Lazi?—a thing agreeing neither with the nature of things nor easy to explain in word.

3.40. Did he not send generals to the Bosporites, who were subject to the Huns, and appropriate the city, though it in no way belonged to him, and make alliance with the rulers of the Ethiopians, of whom the Romans had not even heard at all?
3.41. But he has also encompassed the Homerites and the Red Sea, and adds the Palm-grove to the Roman realm.
3.42. For we forbear to speak of the sufferings of the Libyans and the Italians. The whole earth does not contain the man; it is a small thing for him to rule all men together.
3.43. And he scans the heavens too and searches out the recesses beyond the ocean, wishing to acquire for himself some other inhabited world.
3.44. Why, then, O King, do you still delay? Why are you ashamed of a peace most wretchedly to perish, that he may make you the last morsel of all the rest?
3.45. If you wish to learn what sort of man Justinian would be toward those who yield to him, you have the example near at hand, from ourselves and from the wretched Lazi;
3.46. and if you wish to learn how he is wont to deal with those who are unknown and have done him no wrong at all, consider the Vandals and the Goths and the Moors.

3.47. The chief point has not yet been told. Has he not made it his work in time of peace to get round Alamoundaras, your slave, O most mighty King, by deceit and to detach him from your kingship, and has he not been eager lately to win over the Huns, in no way known to him, against your affairs? And yet no deed more monstrous than this has happened in all time.

3.48. For when he perceived, I think, that the subjugation of the West would all but reach its completion for him, he has now attempted to assail you of the East, since the power of the Persians alone is left him for a contest.
3.49. The peace, then, on his part is already broken for you, and he himself has put an end to the endless treaty.
3.50. For those break the peace not who first take up arms, but who are caught plotting against their neighbours in time of treaty.

3.51. For the charge has been committed by him who attempts it, even if success be absent. But how the war will turn out is plain to everyone, I suppose. For not those who furnish the causes of war, but those who defend themselves against those who furnish them, are ever wont to master the enemy.

3.52. Nor indeed will the contest be for us on equal terms of power. For it chances that the Romans have most of their soldiers at the extremities of the inhabited world, and of two generals, who were their best, we come having killed the one, Sittas, while Justinian will never again see Belisarius. For, neglecting him, he has remained in the West,

3.53. himself holding the Italian dominion. So that, as you go against the enemy, none of all will meet you, and you will have us too, with goodwill, as is likely, and with much experience of the places, leading the way for your army." When Chosroes heard this,

3.54. he was pleased, and calling together whatever was pure among the Persians, he brought out to all both what Vittigis wrote and all that the Armenians said, and set the matter of what should be done before them for counsel.
3.55. There, then, many opinions were spoken tending to either side, but in the end it seemed best that they should make war against the Romans at the beginning of spring.
3.56. For it was the autumn of the year, the thirteenth year of the Emperor Justinian holding the supreme rule.

3.57. The Romans, however, did not suspect this, nor did they think the Persians would ever break the so-called endless treaty, although they had heard that Chosroes both accused their own emperor of his successes in the West and brought against him these charges which I have just mentioned.
4.1. Then too the comet star appeared, at first about as large as a very tall man, but later much greater. And its end was toward the setting sun, its beginning toward the rising,

4.2. and it followed behind the sun itself. For the sun was in Capricorn, and it was in Sagittarius. And some called it the swordfish, because it was very long and had a very sharp point, others the bearded star; and it appeared for more than forty days.

4.3. The wise men in these matters, in no way agreeing with one another, foretold each different things to be signified by this star; but I, writing what came to pass, give to each to infer from the outcomes as he wishes.

4.4. At once a great Hunnic army, crossing the Ister river, fell upon all Europe, a thing that had happened often before, but never bringing so many evils in number or so great in magnitude to the men there. For from the Ionian Gulf these barbarians plundered all in succession as far as the suburbs of Byzantium.
4.5. And they took thirty-two fortresses in Illyricum, and subdued by force the city of Cassandria (which the ancients called Potidaea, so far as we know), not having stormed a wall before.
4.6. And holding the spoils and leading off twelve myriads of captives, they all withdrew home, no opposition meeting them.
4.7. And at a later time, often coming there, they did irreparable dreadful things to the Romans.

4.8. These also stormed the wall in the Chersonese, and forcing those who defended themselves from the wall, and passing over the rampart by way of the surf of the sea—the rampart which is by the so-called Black Gulf—and thus getting within the long walls and falling unexpectedly upon the Romans in the Chersonese, they killed many and enslaved nearly all.

4.9. And a few even crossing the strait between Sestos and Abydos, and plundering the places in Asia, and again turning back to the Chersonese, were conveyed home with the rest of the army and all the booty.

4.10. And in another invasion, plundering the Illyrians and the Thessalians, they attempted to storm the wall at Thermopylae, but the guards in the walls defending themselves most vigorously, searching out the circuits they found, beyond expectation, the path that leads to the mountain which rises there.
4.11. And thus, having destroyed nearly all the Greeks except the Peloponnesians, they withdrew.
4.12. And the Persians not long after, breaking the treaty, wrought upon the Romans of the East deeds which I shall presently relate.
4.13. Belisarius, having destroyed Vittigis the King of the Goths and the Italians, brought him alive to Byzantium. But how the Persian army invaded the land of the Romans I now go on to relate.
4.14. When the Emperor Justinian perceived that Chosroes desired war, he wished to make some exhortation and to draw him from the attempt.
4.15. There chanced to be at Byzantium one come from the city of Daras, Anastasius by name, having repute for intelligence, who had also put down the tyranny lately arisen at Daras.
4.16. This Anastasius, then, Justinian sent to Chosroes, having written a letter;

4.17. and the writing declared as follows: "It is the part of intelligent men, and of those who have sufficiently practised the things of God, to cut off with all their might the springing causes of war, especially toward men who are most friends; but of unintelligent men, and of those who most readily make the things of God hostile to themselves, to contrive occasions of battle and disturbance that in no way exist.
4.18. For to dissolve peace and go to war is no great matter, since the nature of things has held that the basest of practices are easy even for the most dishonoured of men.
4.19. But for men who have ordered war as they purposed to go again to peace is, I think, not easy.

4.20. And yet you charge us with letters not written for the purpose, and have been eager to interpret these now by your own self-willed judgement, not as we wrote them when we devised them, but as it seems to you, desiring to accomplish your designs not without some veil, will profit.

4.21. But it is in our power to show that your Alamoundaras, lately overrunning our land, wrought in time of peace irreparable deeds—captures of places, plundering of money, murders and enslavements of men so great in number—for which it will be needful for you not to accuse us, but to defend yourself.

4.22. For the deeds, not the intentions, declare to neighbours the charges of those who have done wrong. But though these things are so, we have resolved even so to hold to the peace, while we hear that you, desiring war against the Romans, are fashioning charges that in no way belong to us.

4.23. Reasonably; for those who are eager to set right the present shake off even the charges against their friends, pressing as they are, while those whom the law of friendship does not please are eager to provide even pretexts that do not exist.
4.24. But these things would seem to befit not even ordinary men, much less kings.

4.25. But you, leaving these, consider the measure of those who will perish on both sides in the war, and who would justly bear the blame of what shall befall, and reckon the oaths, which, having sworn and received the money, then dishonouring against need, you could not get round by any arts or sophisms; for the divine is by nature mightier than to be deceived by
4.26. all men." When Chosroes saw this brought to him, for the moment he neither answered anything nor dismissed Anastasius, but compelled him to remain there.

5.1. But when the winter was now abating, and the thirteenth year was ending of the Emperor Justinian holding the supreme rule, Chosroes the son of Cabades invaded the land of the Romans with a great army at the beginning of spring, and brilliantly broke the so-called endless peace. And he went, not through the country between the rivers, but keeping the Euphrates on the right.

5.2. On the other side of the river is the last Roman fortress, which is called Circesium, exceedingly strong, since the Aborrhas, a great river, having its outlet there, mingles with the Euphrates, and this fortress lies at the very angle which the meeting of the two rivers makes.
5.3. And another long wall outside the fortress, taking in the land between each river, completes there about Circesium a triangular shape.

5.4. Therefore Chosroes, neither wishing to make trial of so strong a fortress nor purposing to cross the Euphrates river, but to go against the Syrians and the Cilicians, without any delay drove his army forward, and having traversed a journey of about three days for an unencumbered man along the bank of the Euphrates, he came upon the city of Zenobia; which Zenobia once built and, as is likely, gave her name to the city.
5.5. Now Zenobia was the wife of Odonathus, the ruler of the Saracens there, who from of old were in treaty with the Romans.
5.6. This Odonathus recovered for the Romans the realm of the East, which had come under the Medes. But these things took place in former times.

5.7. Chosroes then, coming very near Zenobia, when he learned that the place was not worth account and perceived the country to be uninhabited and destitute of all good things, fearing lest some time spent there should be a hindrance to his great undertakings for no result, made trial of taking the place by agreement. But when nothing went forward, he quickly drove his army on.
5.8. And having again traversed so great a road, he came to the city of Sura, which is by the Euphrates river,

5.9. and coming very near it he halted. There it chanced that the horse on which Chosroes sat both neighed and struck the ground with its foot. The Magi, inferring this, declared that the place would be taken.
5.10. And he, encamping, led the army against the wall as though to storm it.

5.11. There chanced to be a man, Arsaces by name, an Armenian by race, commander of the soldiers there, who, having got the soldiers up onto the battlements and fighting from there most vigorously and killing many of the enemy, was struck by an arrow and died.

5.12. And the Persians then (for it was late in the day), as though they would storm the wall again on the morrow, withdrew to their camp; but the Romans, in despair, since their commander had died, purposed to become suppliants of Chosroes.

5.13. On the following day, then, they sent the bishop of the city to entreat and to beg off the place, who, taking with him some of his attendants bearing fowls and wine and pure loaves, came to Chosroes, and let himself down to the ground and in tears besought him to spare wretched men and a city most dishonoured for the Romans, and held of no account by the Persians, neither in former times nor ever to be hereafter; and he promised that the Surenes would give him ransom worthily of themselves and of the city in which they dwelt.

5.14. But Chosroes was harsh toward the Surenes, because, being the first of all the Romans to fall in with him, they neither received him willingly into the city, but, daring even to take up arms against him, killed a considerable throng of notable Persians.

5.15. He did not, however, bring out his anger, but hid it exactly beneath his face, so that, by making the punishment upon the Surenes, he might render himself terrible and invincible to the Romans. For thus he supposed that those who should ever be in his path would go over to him with no trouble.

5.16. Therefore with much friendliness he raised up the bishop, and receiving the gifts gave a certain impression that he would presently consult with the men of note among the Persians about the ransom of the Surenes and dispose the request well.
5.17. And thus he dismissed the bishop with his attendants, having no perception of the plot, and sent with him some of the notable Persians as escorts, ostensibly in word.

5.18. These he secretly bade go with him up to the wall, encouraging him and lifting him with good hopes, so that he and all those with him might be seen by those within rejoicing and fearing nothing.

5.19. And when the guards, opening the postern, should be about to receive them into the city, throwing some stone or wood between the threshold and the door, they should not allow it to be set, but should themselves stand for some time in the way of those who wished to set it; for the army would not long after follow them.
5.20. Having charged the men these things, Chosroes got his army in readiness, and bade them go at a run against the city whenever he himself should give the signal.

5.21. And when they came very near the wall, the Persians, having saluted the bishop, remained outside; but the Surenes, seeing the man returned overjoyed and escorted with much honour by the enemy, taking no thought of any difficulties, opened the whole postern and received the priest with his attendants, clapping and uttering many blessings.
5.22. And when all had got inside, the guards thrust at the postern as though to set it, but the Persians threw into the middle a stone which had been prepared for them.
5.23. And the guards, thrusting still more and forcing the postern, were by no means able to bring it to the threshold.
5.24. Nor indeed did they dare to open it again, since they perceived that it was held by the enemy. But some say that the Persians threw not a stone but a wood into the postern.

5.25. And while the Surenes had not yet quite perceived the plot, Chosroes was present with his whole army, and the barbarians, forcing the postern, flung it open, and in a short time it was taken by storm.
5.26. At once, then, held by anger, Chosroes plundered the houses, and killing many of the men and reckoning all the rest as slaves and burning the whole city, razed it to the ground.
5.27. And thus he dismissed Anastasius, bidding him report to the Emperor Justinian where in the world he had left Chosroes the son of Cabades.

5.28. After this, held either by humanity or by love of money, or gratifying a woman whom he had taken thence captive, Euphemia by name, and made his wedded wife, being enamoured of her with an extraordinary love (for she was very comely in appearance), Chosroes resolved to do some good thing for the Surenes.

5.29. Sending, then, to Sergiopolis, subject to the Romans, which is named after Sergius an illustrious saint, distant from the captured city a hundred and twenty-six stades and lying toward the south wind of it in the so-called barbarian plain, he bade Candidus the bishop there buy the captives, who were twelve thousand, for two centenaria.

5.30. But he (for he said he had no money) plainly shrank from the affair. Therefore Chosroes thought fit that he, having left in a little book his agreement to give the money at a later time, should thus buy for so little money so great a multitude of slaves.

5.31. And Candidus did accordingly, and agreed to give the gold within a year, having sworn the most dread oaths, and he appointed for himself this penalty: that if he should not give the money within the agreed time, he should give it double, and himself be a priest no longer, as having disregarded what he had sworn.
5.32. Candidus, having written these things in a document, received all the Surenes.
5.33. Of whom a few survived, but the most, not being able to hold out against the hardship that befell them, perished a little later. Having accomplished these things, Chosroes led the army forward.

6.1. A little before, the emperor had chanced to divide the office of General of the East into two, and leaving the part as far as the Euphrates river to the name of Belisarius, who before held the whole command, and entrusting the part from there to the Persian borders to Bouzes, he bade Bouzes take care of the whole command of the East, until Belisarius should return from Italy.
6.2. Therefore Bouzes, having the whole army following him, at first remained at Hierapolis. But when he learned what had befallen the Surenes, calling together the foremost of the

6.3. Hierapolites, he spoke as follows: "For those whose contest against the invaders is on equal terms of power, it is not at all unfitting to come to blows with the enemy straightway; but for those who chance to be far inferior to their adversaries by a great difference, it will be more profitable to get round the enemy by certain devices than, drawing up openly against them, to go into a foreseen danger.

6.4. How great is the army of Chosroes you hear, I suppose. But if he should wish to take us by siege, and we should carry on the war from the wall, it is likely that provisions will fail us, while the Persians will get everything from our land with no one opposing.

6.5. And the siege being thus prolonged, I think the wall will not even suffice against the plots of the enemy, which chances to be most assailable in many places, and something irreparable will befall the Romans.

6.6. But if with one portion of the army we guard the wall of the city, and the rest seize the foothills about the city, overrunning from there now the camp of the adversaries, now those sent out for provisions, they will compel Chosroes very soon to break up the siege and make his withdrawal in a short time, neither able to bring his assaults more fearlessly against the wall nor to provide any of the necessaries for so great an army."
6.7. So much Bouzes said, and seemed to speak what was expedient, but did none of what was needful. For having chosen out whatever was notable in the Roman army,
6.8. he went off. And in what part of the earth he chanced to be, neither any of the Romans in Hierapolis nor the army of the enemy was able to learn. So these things were carried on here.

6.9. And the Emperor Justinian, learning of the Persian inroad, at once sent Germanus, his own nephew, with much tumult, having three hundred followers, and promised that a great army would not long after follow him.

6.10. And Germanus, coming to Antioch, went around the whole wall in a circle, and found most of it strong (for the river Orontes flows past all the part in the level ground, making it impassable for assailants, and the parts in the high ground, held up by precipitous places, were by no means accessible to the enemy), but coming to the height, which the people there have been accustomed to call Orocasias, he perceived that the wall there was most assailable.
6.11. For there happens to be a certain rock there, sufficiently broad for a great extent, but in height a little less than the wall.

6.12. He bade them, then, either, cutting off the rock, make a deep ditch about the wall, lest someone going up from there should come onto the wall, or, building some great tower there, fasten the building from it to the wall of the city.

6.13. But to the architects of the buildings neither of these seemed to be done. For neither would it be completed in a short time, the inroad of the enemy being so pressing, and beginning this work and not coming to its end they would show the enemy nothing else than where in the world the wall should be assailed by them.
6.14. And Germanus, foiled of this idea, at first, awaiting an army from Byzantium, had some hope upon it.

6.15. But when, much time being spent, neither any army came from the emperor nor was it expected to come, he fell into fear lest Chosroes, learning that the emperor's nephew was there, should make it of more importance than anything else to take both Antioch and him, and from this, leaving all else, should go against it with his whole army.
6.16. These things being in the mind of the Antiochenes too, and counsel having been taken about them, it seemed most expedient to escape the present danger by giving money to Chosroes.

6.17. They send, then, Megas, the bishop of Beroea, an intelligent man (for he chanced then to be sojourning among them), to entreat Chosroes; who, dispatched thence, overtakes the army of the Medes not far from Hierapolis.
6.18. And coming into the presence of Chosroes he much entreated him to pity men who neither had wronged him at all nor were able to oppose the Persian army.

6.19. For it befitted a king least of all to trample upon and force those who withdrew and in no way wished to oppose, since not even of what was now being done would anything kingly or noble be wrought by him, in that, not granting the Emperor of the Romans some time for counsel, so as either to confirm the peace, however it should seem to each, or to prepare the matters of war by agreement, as is fitting, but coming thus inconsiderately against the Romans in arms, while their own emperor did not yet know what was befalling them.
6.20. Chosroes, hearing this, was by no means able through his ignorance to be set right in character by intelligent speech, but was lifted in mind still more than before.
6.21. He threatened, then, to subdue all the Syrians and Cilicians, and bidding Megas follow him, led the army to Hierapolis.
6.22. There arriving and encamping, when he saw that the wall was strong and learned that it had a sufficient garrison of soldiers, he asked money of the Hierapolites,

6.23. sending Paul as interpreter to them. This Paul had been reared in the land of the Romans and had gone to a schoolmaster among the Antiochenes, and was said to be a Roman by race from the beginning.

6.24. But they, most of all fearing for the wall, which encompassed a great country up to the mountain that rises there, and then wishing to have their land unravaged, agreed to give two thousand pounds of silver.
6.25. Then Megas, entreating Chosroes on behalf of all the men of the East, did not cease until Chosroes agreed both to receive ten centenaria of gold and to depart from the whole Roman realm.
7.1. Thus, then, on that day Megas, departing thence, drove on toward the Antiochenes, and Chosroes, receiving the ransom, went to Beroea.
7.2. Now Beroea lies between Antioch and Hierapolis, and is distant a journey of two days for an unencumbered man from each.
7.3. Megas, then, journeying with a few men, went more swiftly, while the Persian army always accomplished the half of the road.
7.4. And on the fourth day the one came to Antioch, the other to the suburb of Beroea.

7.5. And Chosroes, having sent Paul, at once demanded money of the Beroeans, not only as much as he had received from the Hierapolites, but double of these, since he saw that their wall was most assailable in many places.

7.6. And the Beroeans (for they had no confidence at all in the wall) with eagerness undertook to give all; but having given two thousand pounds of silver, they said they were not able to give the rest.
7.7. And Chosroes pressing them for this reason, when night came on, they all fled to the fortress which is in the acropolis, together with the soldiers who had been stationed there for guard.

7.8. On the following day some were sent by Chosroes into the city to receive the money, but coming very near the wall they found all the gates shut, and being able to meet no man, they reported to the king their present situation.
7.9. And he bade them, putting ladders to the wall, make trial of the ascent; and they did accordingly.
7.10. And no one opposing them, getting within the wall they opened the gates at their pleasure,

7.11. and received into the city the whole army and Chosroes himself. And the king, now held by much anger, all but burned the whole city. But going up into the acropolis, he resolved to storm the fortress.

7.12. There the Roman soldiers, defending themselves vigorously, killed some of the enemy, but a great piece of good fortune befell Chosroes through the folly of the besieged, who fled into this fortress not alone, but together with their horses and the other animals, and being thus outgeneralled by this pettiness came into danger.
7.13. For there being one spring there, since the horses and mules and other animals drank it out beyond what was needful, the water happened to be dried up. So matters stood for the Beroeans.
7.14. But Megas, coming to Antioch and announcing what he had agreed with Chosroes, by no means persuaded them to carry it out in deed.

7.15. For the Emperor Justinian chanced to have sent John the son of Rufinus and Julian the secretary of secrets as envoys to Chosroes. The Romans call this dignity asecretis; for they have been accustomed to call secret things secreta.

7.16. These, coming to Antioch, remained. And Julian, the one of the envoys, expressly forbade all to give money to the enemy or to buy the emperor's cities, and slandered to Germanus the high-priest Ephraemius, as being eager to hand over the city to Chosroes.
7.17. Therefore Megas withdrew unsuccessful. And Ephraemius, the bishop of Antioch, fearing the Persian inroad, went to Cilicia.
7.18. There Germanus too came not long after, taking a few men, but leaving the most there.

7.19. And Megas, coming quickly to Beroea and being exceedingly grieved at what had befallen, accused Chosroes of having wrought unholy deeds upon the Beroeans, in that, when he had sent him to Antioch as though for the treaty, he had plundered the money of the citizens, who had wronged him in nothing at all, and had compelled them to shut themselves up in this fortress, and thus, burning the city, had razed it needlessly to the ground.

7.20. To this Chosroes answered as follows: "Of these things, comrade, you yourself are the cause, having compelled us to spend time here; for not at the appointed time, but much later than this, have you now arrived.

7.21. And as for the perversity of your citizens, why should one make a long speech, most excellent man? For they, having agreed to give us a fixed sum of silver for their own safety, do not even now think they ought to carry out what was agreed, but thus unrestrainedly, trusting in the strength of the place, disregard us, who are compelled, as you see, I suppose, to undertake a siege of a fortress.
7.22. Whom, indeed, I have hope, with the gods, a little later to punish, and to accomplish upon the guilty the chastisement for the Persians who have needlessly perished before this wall."

7.23. So much Chosroes said, and Megas replies as follows: "If one should consider that, because you are a king, you charge these things upon men wretched and most dishonoured, there is need, gainsaying nothing of what is said, to agree; for to your other power there naturally follows also mastery in argument;
7.24. but if one were permitted, shaking off the rest, to choose the true word, you would have nothing, O King, justly to charge upon us. But hear all gently.

7.25. For I, when I was sent to declare what you enjoined upon the Antiochenes, coming into your presence on the seventh day (than which what could be quicker?), found these things wrought by you upon my fatherland.
7.26. And they, having now lost all their most precious things, then enter only into the contest for their lives, having become, I think, mightier than to bring you any more of their money.
7.27. For to pay something of what is not present would be for a man no device at all.
7.28. And long ago the names of things have been well and rightly distinguished by men; among which is this also, that weakness is separated from ill-will.

7.29. For the latter, going over into resistance through licentiousness of character, is wont, as is likely, to be hated; but the former, carried into this same thing through the impossibility of service, is naturally able to be pitied.
7.30. Allow us, then, O King, who have drawn the worst of all lots, to carry off at least this consolation: that we may not seem to have been ourselves the cause of what has befallen us.
7.31. And think that whatever money you have taken suffices you, measuring it not by your dignity, but looking at the resources of the Beroeans.
7.32. And force us no further, lest you ever seem unable for what you have undertaken; for what is excessive has ever been honoured by the impossible; but not to attempt the impossible is best.
7.33. Let this, then, be my defence for the moment on behalf of these men. But if I should be able to be with the wretched men, I might have something else, now unknown to me,

7.34. to say." So much Megas said, and Chosroes let him go up to the acropolis. And he, coming there and learning all that had befallen concerning the spring, came again in tears to Chosroes, and lying prone insisted that nothing at all of all their money was left to the Beroeans, but besought him to grant them their lives alone.
7.35. And Chosroes, moved by the man's lamentations, carried out the request, and swearing to all in the acropolis gave them pledges.
7.36. And the Beroeans, having come to so great a danger, left the acropolis unharmed and departed each where he wished.

7.37. But of the soldiers a few followed them, while the most came willingly as deserters to Chosroes, charging that the treasury owed them their pay for a long time, and afterward went with him to the country of the Persians.
8.1. And Chosroes (for Megas declared that he had by no means persuaded the Antiochenes to give money) went against them with his whole army.

8.2. And some of the Antiochenes, rising up thence with their money, fled each as he could. This same thing all the rest too purposed, had not, coming in the meanwhile, the commanders of the soldiers in Lebanon, Theoctistus and Molatzes, with six thousand men, encouraged them with hopes and prevented it.
8.3. There not long after the Persian army too came. And all encamped there, bivouacking by the river Orontes and not far from it.

8.4. And Chosroes, sending Paul to the wall, asked the Antiochenes for money, on condition that he would depart thence for ten centenaria of gold; and it was clear that he would receive even less than these at his withdrawal.
8.5. And then the envoys, coming to Chosroes and having said much about the breaking of the peace and heard much from him, withdrew.

8.6. On the following day the populace of the Antiochenes (for they are not earnest, but given enough to jests and disorder) insulted Chosroes much from the battlements and mocked him with unseemly laughter.

8.7. And when Paul came near the wall, advising them to buy themselves and the city for a little money, they all but shot and killed him, had he not, foreseeing it, guarded himself. Therefore, seething with anger, Chosroes resolved to storm the wall.

8.8. On the morrow, then, leading all the Persians against the wall, he bade some assault one part of the river, others another, while he himself, having the most and best, assaulted the height. For there, as I said before, the wall was most assailable.

8.9. There the Romans (for the building on which they were to stand and fight was very narrow) devised the following. Binding long beams to one another, they hung them between the towers, and thus made these spaces far broader, so that still more might be able to defend themselves from there against those storming the wall.
8.10. The Persians, then, pressing most vigorously, sent many arrows from all sides, and especially over the height of the rock.
8.11. And the Romans defended themselves with all their might, not soldiers only, but also many most daring young men of the populace.

8.12. And those storming the wall there seemed to enter the battle on equal terms with the enemy. For the rock, being broad and high and as it were set over against the wall, made the engagement as though on level ground.

8.13. And if anyone of the Roman army had taken courage to get with three hundred men outside the wall and, anticipating, to seize that rock and from there to defend himself against the assailants, never, I think, would the city have come into any danger from the enemy.

8.14. For the barbarians would have had no place from which to storm the wall, being shot from above both from the rock and from the wall. But now (for the Antiochenes had to perish by this Median army) this came into the mind of no one.

8.15. The Persians, then (since Chosroes was present with them and urging them on with a great shout), forcing themselves beyond their strength and giving the adversaries no opportunity to look about or guard against the shots of arrows, and the Romans defending themselves still more with much multitude and tumult, the ropes by which the beams were bound, not bearing the weight, suddenly broke, and together with the beams all who stood on them fell to the ground with a great crash.

8.16. When the other Romans who were fighting from the adjoining towers perceived this, and being by no means able to infer what had happened, but thinking that the wall there was destroyed, they rushed to flight.

8.17. The many young men of the populace, then, who before had been wont to be at faction with one another in the hippodromes, when they came down from the wall, by no means fled, but remained there, while the soldiers, together with Theoctistus and Molatzes, at once leaping onto their horses, which chanced to be prepared there, rode off to the gates, spreading the report that Bouzes was coming with an army, and that they wished quickly both to receive him into the city and together with him to defend against the enemy.
8.18. There many men of the Antiochenes, and all the women with their children, went at a great run to the gates; then, thrust by the horses, in much narrowness they fell.
8.19. And the soldiers, sparing none at all of those in their way, drove still more than before over the fallen, and a great slaughter took place there, especially at the gates themselves.

8.20. And the Persians, no one opposing them, putting ladders to the wall, climbed up with no trouble. And getting quickly onto the battlements, they were for some time by no means willing to come down, but seemed to be looking about and at a loss, suspecting, it seems to me, an ambush of the enemy in the difficult ground.
8.21. For the part within the wall, going straight down from the height, is uninhabited for a great extent. Very high rocks rise there and precipitous places.
8.22. And some say that the delay of the Persians came about by Chosroes' purpose.

8.23. For when he perceived the difficult ground and saw the soldiers fleeing, he feared lest by some necessity, turning back from their retreat, they should cause him trouble, and become a hindrance, should it so chance, to taking a city ancient and worthy of account and the first of the Romans of all the cities in the East, in wealth and size and population and beauty and all other prosperity.

8.24. For which, reckoning all else of less account, he wished to grant the Roman soldiers opportunity, that they might use their flight at their pleasure. Therefore the Persians, signalling with their hands to the fugitives, urged them to flee as quickly as possible.
8.25. The Roman soldiers, then, with their commanders, all departed by the gate that leads to Daphne, the suburb of the Antiochenes;
8.26. for from this gate alone, the others being seized, the Persians refrained; and a few of the populace escaped with the soldiers.
8.27. But when the Persians saw all the Roman soldiers gone forward, coming down from the height they got into the middle of the city.

8.28. There many young men of the Antiochenes, coming to blows with them, at first seemed to have the upper hand in the engagement. Some of them were heavy-armed, but the most were unarmed and used only casts of stones.
8.29. And thrusting back the enemy, they raised the paean and cried out for the Emperor Justinian as gloriously victorious, as though they had conquered.

8.30. Meanwhile Chosroes, sitting in a tower at the height, wishing to say something, sent for the envoys. And one of the commanders, Zabergan, thinking that he wished to come to a parley with the envoys about an agreement, came quickly into the king's

8.31. presence and spoke as follows: "You do not seem to me, O master, to have the same mind toward the Romans concerning their safety as they have. For they both before the danger insult your kingship and, defeated, dare the impossible and do irreparable deeds against the Persians, as though fearing lest some account of humanity should be left them with you; while you wish to pity those who do not think fit to be saved, and have been eager to spare those who in no way wish it.
8.32. And these men, having set an ambush in a captured city, are destroying the victors by certain snares, although all
8.33. the soldiers have long since fled from them." When Chosroes heard this, he sent many of the best against them, who, returning not long after, reported that nothing untoward had befallen.

8.34. For the Persians, forcing the Antiochenes by their multitude, had already routed them, and a great slaughter took place there. For the Persians, sparing no age, killed all in their way down to the boys.

8.35. Then, they say, two women of the notable Antiochenes happened to be outside the wall, and perceiving that they would come under the enemy (for already, going about everywhere, the Persians were seen), came at a run to the river Orontes, and fearing lest the Persians should do some outrage to their bodies, veiling their faces with their head-coverings and casting themselves into the stream of the river, vanished. So every kind of evil held the Antiochenes.

9.1. There Chosroes said to the envoys as follows: "I think the ancient saying is not far from the truth, that God does not give good things unalloyed, but mingling them with evils then furnishes them to men.

9.2. And on this account we do not even have laughter without weeping, but ever some misfortune is fastened beside our good fortunes, and grief beside our pleasures, not allowing anyone ever truly to enjoy the prosperity given.
9.3. For this city, said and being most worthy of account in the land of the Romans, I was able to take with the least trouble, God having improvised the victory for us, as you see, I suppose.
9.4. Yet seeing a slaughter of men so great in number, and the trophy dipped in much blood, no perception of pleasure from the deed has come to me.

9.5. And of these things the wretched Antiochenes are the cause, who, when the Persians stormed the wall, were not able to thrust them back, but against men already victorious and who had taken the city at the first shout, with senseless, death-seeking boldness resolved to grapple.

9.6. All the men of note among the Persians, troubling me much, thought fit that I should net the city and destroy all the captives; but I bade the fugitives rush still more into their retreat, that they might be saved as quickly as possible. For to trample upon the captured is not
9.7. holy." So much Chosroes said, playing the wonder-worker and dissembling to the envoys; yet he did not escape their notice for what reason he granted the opportunity to the fleeing Romans.

9.8. For he was the most clever of all men at saying things that were not and concealing things that were true, and at bringing upon the wronged the charges of his own misdeeds; and besides, ready to agree to everything and to confirm the agreement with an oath, but exceedingly readier to come to forgetfulness of what he had lately agreed and sworn; and for the sake of money ready without shrinking to let his soul down to every defilement, but a simple expert at fashioning piety with his face, and at disavowing in word the deed.

9.9. He who got round the Surenes too, who had done him no wrong at all before, by treachery, and destroyed them in the manner described, when, as the city was being taken, he saw a woman, decorous and not obscure, dragged by the left hand by one of the barbarians with much violence, but unwilling to let go a child which had just been weaned from her, and dragging it with the other hand as it fell to the ground, since it was not able to run with her this violent run—there too displayed his own character.

9.10. For they say that he, groaning ostensibly in word and giving an impression that he was in tears to those then present, both others and Anastasius the envoy, prayed God to punish the author of the evils that had happened.
9.11. And he wished to point obliquely at Justinian the Emperor of the Romans, knowing well that he himself was the most to blame of all.

9.12. Using so great a perversity of nature, Chosroes became King of the Persians (the demon having maimed the eye of Zames, who by his age bore the chief claim to the kingship, after Caoses, whom Cabades hated for no reason), and with no trouble mastered those who rose against him, and easily wrought upon the Romans whatever evils he devised.

9.13. For Fortune, wishing ever to make some man great, accomplishes at the fitting times what she has resolved, nothing opposing the rush of her will, neither considering the man's worth nor reckoning that anything unfitting may come to be, nor that many will blaspheme her for these things, mocking what has come to one beyond his desert who has obtained her favour, nor putting any other of all things in mind, provided only that what seems good to her be accomplished. But let these things be as is dear to God.

9.14. Chosroes bade the army take alive and enslave the survivors of the Antiochenes and plunder all the money, while he himself, with the envoys, went down from the height to the temple which they call a church.
9.15. There Chosroes found treasures of gold and silver so great in number that, taking nothing else of the booty except these treasures, he departed clothed with a magnitude of wealth.
9.16. And taking thence many marvellous marbles, he bade them be set outside the wall, that these too might be conveyed to the country of the Persians.
9.17. Having accomplished these things, he charged the Persians to burn the whole city. And the envoys begged him to refrain from the church alone, of which he had received sufficient ransom.

9.18. And he, having conceded this to the envoys, bade them burn all the rest, and leaving a few there to set fire to the city, himself with all the rest withdrew to the camp where they had bivouacked before.

10.1. Some time before this disaster God, displaying a portent to those dwelling there, signified what was to be. For the standards of the soldiers, who are settled there from of old, before standing toward the setting sun, of their own accord turned and stood toward the rising sun, and again returned to their former position, no one touching them.

10.2. These things the soldiers showed to many others very near at hand and to the paymaster of the camp's expense, while the standards were still shaking. This was a man, Tatian by name, most intelligent, coming from Mopsuestia.

10.3. But not even so did those who saw this portent know that from the emperor of the West to the emperor of the East the rule of the place would pass, so that, plainly, they might by no means be able to escape those who had to suffer what came to pass.

10.4. And I grow dizzy writing of so great a disaster and handing it down to memory for the time to come, and I cannot know what in the world God can wish in raising the affairs of a man or of a place to a height, and then again throwing them down and destroying them from no cause apparent to us.

10.5. For it is not lawful to say of Him that all things do not always come to pass according to reason—He who then endured to see Antioch brought down to the ground by a most unholy man, whose beauty and magnificence in all things not even now could be altogether hidden.
10.6. The church, then, was left alone when the city was destroyed, by the labour and forethought of the Persians on whom this task lay.

10.7. There were left too, about the so-called Cerataeum, many houses, not by any man's forethought, but since they lay somewhere at the extremities of the city, no other building joined to them, the fire was by no means able to reach them.
10.8. And the barbarians burned also the parts outside the wall, except the temple dedicated to Saint Julian, and the houses which chance to be about this temple.
10.9. For there it befell the envoys to lodge. From the wall, however, the Persians refrained altogether.

10.10. A little later the envoys, coming again to Chosroes, spoke as follows: "If the words were not made to you present, O King, we should never have thought that Chosroes the son of Cabades had come in arms into the land of the Romans, dishonouring the oaths lately sworn by you—which seems the last and strongest of all things among men, the pledge of mutual faith and truth—and dissolving the treaties, whose hope alone is left to those who through ill fortune in war do not live in safety.
10.11. For one might say that such a thing is nothing else than that the life of men has been changed into that of beasts.
10.12. For in never making treaties, war will be left altogether endless, and war that has no end is by nature wont ever to remove from their nature those who use it.

10.13. And what did you mean, writing a little before to your brother that he himself was the cause of the breaking of the treaties? Is it not clear that you agree the breaking of treaties to be a very great evil?

10.14. If, then, he wronged you in nothing, you do not now justly come against us; but if it chances that something of the kind was wrought by your brother, yet let the charge against you too have been accomplished thus far and no further, that you yourself may seem the better. For he who is worsted in evils,

10.15. this man would justly conquer in better things. And yet we know well that the Emperor Justinian has never opposed the peace, and we beg you not to work such evils upon the Romans, from which there will be no profit for the Persians, but you will gain only this, that you have needlessly wrought irreparable deeds upon those who have lately made a treaty with you." So much the envoys said.

10.16. And Chosroes, hearing this, insisted that the treaty had been broken by the Emperor Justinian, and recounted the causes which the latter had furnished, some of them worthy of account, but others paltry and fashioned for no reason; and most of all he thought fit to show that his letters were most to blame for the war, those written to Alamoundaras and the Huns, as I have said in the foregoing.
10.17. That a Roman man, however, had invaded the land of the Persians or displayed deeds of war, he could neither say nor show.
10.18. The envoys, however, in part did not refer the causes to Justinian, but to some of those who had served him, and in part fastened on what was said as not having happened so.
10.19. In the end Chosroes thought fit that the Romans give him much money, but advised that they should not, by furnishing the money for the moment only, wish to confirm the peace for all time.
10.20. For the friendship that arises among men on the basis of money is for the most part spent together with the money as it is consumed.

10.21. The Romans, then, must pay the Persians a fixed yearly sum. "For thus," he said, "the Persians will have the peace with them firm, themselves guarding the Caspian Gates and no longer vexed with them on account of the city of Daras, for which they too will be ever paid." "Then," the envoys said,
10.22. "the Persians wish to hold the Romans tributary for the payment of tribute." "No,

10.23. but the Romans shall have for the future their own soldiers, the Persians," Chosroes said, "furnishing them a fixed wage for the service; since you furnish to certain of the Huns and to the Saracens too a yearly gold, not being tributary to them, but that they may guard your land unravaged for all

10.24. time." Chosroes and the envoys, having discussed many such things with one another, came to terms afterward, on condition that Chosroes, having received for the moment fifty centenaria from the Romans and carrying off five others as a yearly tax for all time, should do them no further harm, but should himself, having received hostages from the envoys on this agreement, make his withdrawal with the whole army to his native land; and that there envoys sent by the Emperor Justinian should henceforth establish the compacts concerning the peace in security.

11.1. Then Chosroes went to Seleucia, a city on the sea, distant from Antioch a hundred and thirty stades, and there, neither finding nor harming any Roman, bathed alone in the water of the sea, and having sacrificed to the sun and to whatever others he wished, and invoked the gods much, rode back.
11.2. And coming to the camp, he said that he had a certain desire to view the city of the Apameans, being in the neighbourhood, for no other reason than for the sake of inquiry.

11.3. And the envoys conceded this too, unwillingly, on condition, however, that he, having viewed the city and carried off from there a thousand pounds of silver, should harm nothing else and ride back.

11.4. But it was clear to the envoys and to all the rest that Chosroes was setting out for Apamea for this reason only: that, taking hold of some pretext of no account, he might plunder both it and the country there. Then he went up to Daphne, the suburb of Antioch.
11.5. There he marvelled greatly at the grove and the springs of water;

11.6. for both are tolerably worth seeing. And having sacrificed to the nymphs, he departed, harming nothing else, but burning the temple of the archangel Michael together with certain other houses, for the following cause.

11.7. A Persian man, riding a horse, notable in the Persian army and known to King Chosroes, came to a precipitous place about the so-called Tretus with certain others, where there is a temple of the archangel Michael, the work of Evaris.
11.8. This man, seeing one of the Antiochene young men, on foot and alone, hiding there, pursued him apart from the others. The young man was a butcher,

11.9. Aeimachus by name. He, when he was about to be overtaken, suddenly turning, struck the pursuer with a stone, and hit him on the forehead at the temple by the ear. And he fell at once to the ground, but the youth, drawing his scimitar, killed the man.
11.10. And having stripped him at his pleasure of his arms and all his gold and whatever else he chanced to be wearing, and leaping onto the horse, he drove forward.
11.11. And whether by chance or using experience of the places, he was wholly able to escape the notice of the enemy and to flee.
11.12. Chosroes, learning this and exceedingly grieved at what had befallen, bade some of his followers burn the temple of the archangel of which I spoke before.
11.13. And they, thinking that this was that one, burned it together with the buildings about it, and supposed that they had carried out the commands of Chosroes. So these things were thus.

11.14. And Chosroes went with his whole army toward Apamea. Now there is in Apamea a piece of wood a cubit long, a part of the cross on which Christ in Jerusalem once endured, it is agreed, his not unwilling punishment, brought there secretly in ancient time by a Syrian man.

11.15. And the men of old, believing that it would be a great safeguard for themselves and for the city, having made a wooden case for it, deposited it, which they adorned with much gold and precious stones, and handed it to three priests, that they should guard it with all safety, and bringing it out every year they do obeisance to it on one day, all the people together.

11.16. Then, therefore, the people of the Apameans, when they learned that the army of the Medes was coming against them, were in great fear. And hearing that Chosroes by no means told the truth, and coming to Thomas the high-priest of the city, they begged him to show them the wood of the cross, that, having done obeisance to it for the last time, they might die.

11.17. And he did accordingly. Then a sight came to pass there mightier than word and belief. For the priest, bearing the wood, displayed it, and above it a gleam of fire was carried, and the part of the roof over it was lit with much light beyond the wonted.
11.18. And as the priest walked everywhere in the temple, the gleam went forward with him, ever keeping the place of the roof above it.
11.19. And the populace of the Apameans, from the pleasure of the wonder, were astonished and rejoiced and wept, and already all had confidence about their safety.

11.20. And Thomas, when he had gone around the whole temple, depositing the wood of the cross in the case, covered it, and the gleam suddenly ceased. And learning that the army of the enemy had come very near the city, with much haste he came to Chosroes.
11.21. And he, when he inquired of the priest whether the Apameans wished to oppose the Median army from the wall, Thomas answered that no such thing had come into the men's mind.
11.22. "Then," said Chosroes, "receive me into the city with a few men, all the gates being thrown
11.23. open." The priest said, "For to this very thing I have come to invite you." The whole army, then, encamped, bivouacking before the wall.

11.24. And Chosroes, choosing out two hundred of the best men among the Persians, rode into the city. But when he was inside the gates, he forgot of his own will what he had agreed with the envoys, and bade the bishop give not a thousand pounds of silver only, nor ten times these, but also the treasures that chanced to be deposited there, all the gold and silver, being prodigiously great.
11.25. And I think he would not have shrunk from enslaving and plundering the whole city, had not something divine manifestly hindered him.
11.26. So greatly did love of money astound him, and his desire of glory turned his mind.
11.27. For he thought the enslavements of cities a great glory for himself, making nothing at all of it if, disregarding treaties and compacts, he wrought such things upon the Romans.

11.28. This purpose of Chosroes will be declared by what he attempted about the city of Daras in this very retreat, holding the agreements in all disregard, and what he did to the Callinicenses a little later in time of peace, which shall be told in the books to follow. But God, as has been said,

11.29. preserved Apamea. And when Chosroes had taken all the treasures, and Thomas saw him now drunk with the abundance of money, bringing out the wood of the cross together with the case and opening the case and displaying the wood, he said, "O most mighty King, these alone are left to me of all my treasures.

11.30. The case, then (for it is adorned with gold and precious stones), there is no grudging that you take it together with all the rest; but this wood, which is saving and precious to us—this, I beseech you and entreat, give to me." So much the priest said. And Chosroes conceded it and carried out the request.
11.31. Afterward, using much ambition, he bade the populace go up into the hippodrome and the charioteers contend in their wonted fashion.

11.32. There too he himself went up and was eager to be a spectator of what was done. But since he had heard much before that the Emperor Justinian was extraordinarily devoted to the Blue colour, which is dark blue, wishing to go against him here too, he wished to fit the victory to the Green.
11.33. The charioteers, then, beginning from the starting-line, set to work, and some chance befell him who was clothed in Blue to drive past and go in front.
11.34. And he who was clad in the Green colour followed him in the same track.

11.35. And Chosroes, thinking this had happened on purpose, was vexed and with a threat cried out that the Caesar had needlessly gone in front of the rest, and bade the horses going in front be checked, so that for the rest they should contend behind; and when this had been done as he bade, so both Chosroes and the Green party seemed to win.
11.36. Then one of the Apameans, coming into the presence of Chosroes, accused a Persian man of having gone up into his house and forcing his daughter, who was a virgin.
11.37. And he, hearing this and seething with anger, bade the man be led off. And when he was present, he charged that he be impaled in the camp.

11.38. And the populace, learning this, cried out with all their might extraordinarily, begging the man off from the king's anger. And Chosroes agreed to release the man to them, but secretly impaled him not long after. Having accomplished these things, he rode back with his whole army.

12.1. But when he came to the city of Chalcis, distant from the city of Beroea eighty-four stades, again he came to a certain forgetfulness of the agreements, and encamping not far from the wall, he sent Paul to threaten the Chalcidians that he would take the city by siege, unless they should purchase safety by giving ransom and hand over to him as many soldiers as chanced to be there together with their commander.

12.2. And the Chalcidians, having fallen into great fear of each king, swore that no soldiers at all were dwelling among them, though they had hidden both others and Adonachus the commander of the soldiers in certain little houses, that they might not be manifest to the enemy; and having with difficulty collected two centenaria of gold, since they dwelt in a city not very prosperous, by giving Chosroes their lives they saved both the city and themselves.
12.3. From there Chosroes no longer wished to make his retreat by the way he had come, but to cross the Euphrates river and plunder as much money as possible from Mesopotamia.

12.4. Having, then, yoked a bridge about the place Obbane, which is distant from the fortress at Barbalissus forty stades, he himself crossed and bade his whole army cross as quickly as possible, intimating that he would loose the bridge on the third day, and fixing also the time of the day.
12.5. And when the appointed time came, it chanced that some of the army were left behind, not having yet crossed, but he, reckoning nothing at all, sent those who should loose the bridge.
12.6. And those left behind, each as he could, went up to their native land. Then a certain ambition came upon Chosroes to take the city of Edessa.
12.7. For a saying of the Christians urged him to this and gnawed at his mind, because they insisted that it was impregnable, for the following cause.

12.8. There was, in ancient time, a certain Augarus, toparch of Edessa (for so they then called the kings of each nation). This Augarus was the most intelligent of all the men of his time, and from this most friendly to the Emperor Augustus.

12.9. For, wishing to be in treaty with the Romans, he came to Rome, and coming to a parley with Augustus, so astonished him by his surpassing intelligence that Augustus no longer wished to let go of his company, but was straightway a burning lover of his conversation, and whenever he met him, by no means wished to part from him.
12.10. Much time, then, was spent by him in this absence from home. And once, wishing to go to his native land and being by no means able to persuade Augustus to let him go,

12.11. he devised the following. He set out as though to hunt in the places about Rome; for he chanced to have a certain earnest practice about these things. And going about much country, he hunted many of the wild beasts there alive, and gathering up earth from the ground, he carried it from each region; and thus he returned to Rome, having both the earth and the beasts.

12.12. Augustus, then, going up into the hippodrome, sat as he was wont, and Augarus, coming into his presence, showed him the earth and the beasts, recounting from what region each earth and each of the beasts was.
12.13. Then he bade them set the earth in different places of the hippodrome, and gathering all the beasts into one place, then to release them.
12.14. The attendants, then, did accordingly. And the beasts, separating from one another, went to that earth which chanced to be from the region whence each had been taken.

12.15. And Augustus watched what was done exactly for a long time, and marvelled that nature, untaught, makes its native earth desirable to the animals. And Augarus, suddenly taking hold of his knees,
12.16. said, "What mind, O master, do you think I have, who have a wife and children and a kingdom—small, indeed, but in my native land?"
12.17. And he, worsted by the truth of the word and constrained, conceded that he should depart, unwillingly, and bade him ask for whatever he needed.
12.18. And when Augarus had obtained this, he begged Augustus to build him a hippodrome in the city of Edessa. And he conceded this too. Thus, departing from Rome, Augarus came to Edessa.

12.19. And his citizens inquired of him whether he came bringing them some good thing from the Emperor Augustus. And he, answering, said that he brought the Edessenes a grief without penalty and a joy without gain, intimating the fortune of the hippodrome.

12.20. At a later time Augarus, having come far on in age, was seized with a certain grievous gout exceedingly. Distressed, then, by the pains and the immobility thence, he brought the matter to the physicians, and gathered from every land all the wise men in these things.
12.21. From whom afterward (for they were not able to find any cure of the evil) he stood off, and falling into helplessness lamented his present fortune.

12.22. And about that time Jesus, the Son of God, being in the body, was conversing with the men in Palestine, and by never sinning at all, but also accomplishing the impossible, was manifestly displaying that He was truly the Son of God;

12.23. for calling the dead He raised them as from sleep, and opened the eyes of those born thus maimed, and cleansed leprosies of the whole body and loosed maiming of the feet, and all the other afflictions which by physicians are named incurable.

12.24. These things being announced by those from Palestine sojourning in Edessa, Augarus heard, and took courage, and writing a letter to Jesus begged Him to depart from Judaea and from the senseless men there, and for the rest to live with him.
12.25. When Christ saw this brought to Him, He wrote back to Augarus, plainly refusing that He would come, but promising health by the letter.

12.26. And they say He added this too, that the city would never be taken by barbarians.
