This conclusion of the letter those who wrote the history of that time by no means knew; for they did not anywhere mention it; but the Edessenes say they found it together with the letter, so that indeed they have set up the letter thus inscribed instead of any other safeguard in the gates of the city.
12.27. The city, then, did come under the Medes at a later time, not taken, however, but in the following manner.

12.28. When Augarus received the writing of Christ, he became a little later free of evils, and living in health for a long time died; but whoever of his children succeeded to the kingdom, having become the most unholy of all men, both wronged his subjects in many ways and, fearing the punishment from the Romans, went over willingly to the Persians.
12.29. And much later the Edessenes, having killed the barbarian guards dwelling among them, handed over the city to the Romans.

12.30. And once a thought came to me, that if Christ wrote not what was said, but because men came to this belief, He wishes on this account to guard the city impregnable, that He might give them no pretext of error. But let these things be as is dear to God, and so be said.

12.31. To Chosroes, then, it seemed of importance for these reasons to take Edessa. And when he came to Batnae, a town small and of no account, distant a day's journey from Edessa, there he bivouacked that night, and at deep dawn drove with his whole army toward Edessa.
12.32. And it befell them, falling into a wandering, to bivouac on the next day in the same place;

12.33. which, they say, befell them even twice. And when Chosroes with difficulty came very near Edessa, they say that a flux fell upon his face and his jaw was swollen. Therefore he by no means wished to make trial of the city, but sending Paul asked the Edessenes for money.
12.34. And they said they feared not at all for the city, but, that he might not harm their lands, agreed to give two centenaria of gold. And he received the money and kept the agreement.
13.1. Then too the Emperor Justinian wrote a letter to Chosroes, agreeing to carry out the things agreed by him and the envoys concerning the peace.
13.2. When Chosroes saw this brought to him, he released the hostages and was preparing for departure, and wished to give back all the captives of the Antiochenes.

13.3. When the Edessenes learned this, they displayed an eagerness mightier than report. For there was no one who did not bring his ransom to the church for these captives, according to the measure of his substance.

13.4. And there were those by whom this was done even beyond measure. For the courtesans, taking off the adornment they had on their bodies, threw it there, and if any husbandman lacked furniture or silver but had an ass or a sheep, he brought it to the church with much haste.
13.5. There was gathered, then, a very great quantity of gold and silver and other goods,

13.6. but nothing was given for ransom. For Bouzes chanced to be present there, who undertook to hinder the thing, awaiting that some great gain would come to him from it. Therefore Chosroes, taking all the captives with him, went forward.
13.7. The Carrhenes met him, offering much money; but he said it did not belong to them, since the most were not Christians but happened to be of the old faith.

13.8. And indeed he received money even from the Constantinians, though saying that the city belonged to him from his fathers. For when Cabades took Amida, he wished to take Edessa and Constantina too.
13.9. But coming near Edessa he inquired of the Magi whether the city would be taken by him, showing them the place with his right hand.
13.10. And they said the city would be taken by no device, inferring that, by stretching out his right hand to it, he gave a sign not of capture or any other hardship, but of safety.
13.11. And he, hearing this, was persuaded and led the army against Constantina.
13.12. And coming there he charged his whole army to encamp as though to besiege it.

13.13. Now the priest of Constantina then was Baradotus, a man just and most dear to God, and from this having his prayer ever effective for whatever he wished; whose very face anyone seeing would at once have inferred that the man was most continually pleasing to God.

13.14. This Baradotus then, coming to Cabades, brought wine and dried figs and honey and pure loaves, and begged him not to make trial of a city which is of no account and has been much neglected by the Romans, having neither garrison of soldiers nor any other safeguard, but only its inhabitants, wretched men.

13.15. So he spoke; and Cabades agreed to grant him the city and gifted him with all the provisions which had been prepared for the camp for the siege, being prodigiously great; and thus he departed from the land of the Romans. Therefore Chosroes thought fit that the city belonged to him from his fathers.
13.16. And coming to Daras he undertook a siege. And within the Romans and Martin the general (for he chanced to be there) prepared for resistance.

13.17. The city is encompassed by two walls, of which the inner is great and simply worth seeing (for each tower rises to a height of a hundred feet, and the rest of the wall sixty); but the outer is much smaller, yet otherwise strong and worth much account.
13.18. And the space between has a breadth of not less than fifty feet; here the Darenes are wont to put their oxen and the other animals when the enemy press upon them.
13.19. At first, then, Chosroes, making an assault on the western part of the wall and forcing it by a multitude of arrows, burned the gates of the short wall.

13.20. None of the barbarians, however, dared to get inside. Then he resolved to make a tunnel secretly to the eastern part of the city. For there only can the earth be dug, since the rest of the wall was built by its makers on rock.
13.21. The Persians, then, beginning from the ditch, dug. And it being very deep, they were neither seen by the enemy nor gave them any perception of what was being done.

13.22. They had already gone under the foundations of the outer wall, and were about, getting into the space between each wall a little later and passing the great wall too, to take the city by storm; but (for it was not destined that it be taken by the Persians) one from the camp of Chosroes about midday came alone very near the wall, whether a man or something else mightier than a man, and gave to those who saw him an impression that he was gathering the arrows which the Romans had a little before shot from the wall against the troublesome barbarians.

13.23. And doing this and holding his shield before him, he seemed to mock those on the battlements and to jest with laughter. Then, declaring to them the whole matter, he bade all keep awake and take care of their safety as much as possible.
13.24. And having signified this he departed, and the Romans with much tumult and disturbance bade men dig in the space between each wall.
13.25. And the Persians, indeed, not knowing what was being done, none the less set to work.

13.26. The barbarians, then, making a straight path below toward the wall of the city, and the Romans, by the purpose of Theodorus, a man learned in the so-called mechanical science, making the trench crosswise and of sufficient depth, it befell the Persians, getting into the middle between the two walls, suddenly to fall into the Roman tunnel.
13.27. And the foremost of them the Romans killed, while those behind, fleeing quickly, were saved in the camp. For the Romans by no means resolved to pursue them in the dark.

13.28. Chosroes, then, having failed in this attempt and despairing for the rest of taking the city by any device, came to a parley with the besieged, and having received a thousand pounds of silver, went to the country of the Persians.

13.29. When the Emperor Justinian learned this, he no longer wished to carry out what had been agreed, charging Chosroes that he had attempted to take the city of Daras in time of peace. These things befell the Romans in the first inroad of Chosroes, and the summer was ending.

14.1. And Chosroes, having built a city in Assyria, in a place distant a day's journey from the city of Ctesiphon, named it the Antioch of Chosroes, and settled there all the captives of the Antiochenes, for whom he prepared a bath and a hippodrome and arranged that they should have all other luxuries.
14.2. For he brought with him both the charioteers and the craftsmen of musical works from Antioch and the other Roman cities.

14.3. And besides he fed these Antiochenes at public expense more carefully than befits captives for all time, and thought fit that they should be called royal, so that they should be subject to none of the magistrates but to the king alone.

14.4. And if any other Roman, having become a runaway, was able to escape to the Antioch of Chosroes, and someone called him a kinsman of those dwelling there, it was no longer permitted to the owner to lead this captive away, not even if the one who had enslaved the man happened to be among the very notable Persians.

14.5. For the Antiochenes the portent which befell in the reign of Anastasius ended in this outcome. For then a hard wind suddenly fell upon the suburb of Daphne, and the cypresses there, which were exceedingly tall, were overturned from their lowest roots and fell to the ground, which the law by no means allowed to be cut.

14.6. A little later, when Justin ruled the Romans, an earthquake exceedingly violent both shook the whole city and brought most and the fairest of the buildings at once to the ground, and they say that then three hundred thousand of the Antiochenes perished.
14.7. And in this capture the whole city, as I have said, was destroyed. So the suffering of the Antiochenes turned out thus.

14.8. And Belisarius came to the emperor at Byzantium summoned from Italy, and the emperor, when he had wintered in Byzantium, sent him as general against Chosroes and the Persians at the beginning of spring, together with the commanders who had come with him from Italy, of whom he bade one, Valerian, lead the troops in Armenia.
14.9. For Martin chanced to have been sent straightway to the East, and on this account Chosroes,
14.10. as has been shown, found him at Daras. Of the Goths, Vittigis remained at Byzantium, but all the rest made the expedition against Chosroes with Belisarius.
14.11. Then one of the envoys of Vittigis, the one who laid claim to the name of bishop, died in the country of the Persians, but the other remained there.

14.12. And the interpreter who followed them withdrew to the land of the Romans, and John, who commanded the soldiers in Mesopotamia, seizing him about the borders of Constantina and leading him into the city, shut him up in prison, who brought out to him there everything he inquired about what had been done.
14.13. So these things turned out thus. And Belisarius with his followers went quickly, being eager to anticipate before Chosroes should make another inroad into the land of the Romans.
15.1. Meanwhile Chosroes led his army against Colchis, the Lazi bringing him on for the following cause.

15.2. The Lazi at first dwelt in Colchis, being subject to the Romans, not, however, for the payment of tribute, nor obeying them in any other command, except that, whenever their king died, the Emperor of the Romans sent the tokens of rule to him who should succeed to the kingship.

15.3. And he guarded the borders of the country together with his subjects exactly, lest the hostile Huns from the Caucasus, which is their neighbour, journeying through Lazica should invade the land of the Romans.
15.4. And they kept guard neither receiving money or an army from the Romans nor making any expedition together with the Romans, but ever trading by sea with the Romans dwelling on the Pontus.
15.5. For they themselves have neither salt nor grain nor any other good thing, but furnishing skins and hides and slaves, they got their necessaries.

15.6. But when the affairs of Gourgenes the king of the Iberians came to be as I have said before, Roman soldiers began to sojourn among the Lazi, with whom these barbarians were vexed, and most of all with the general Peter, who was given to insulting those he met.

15.7. This Peter came from Arzanene, which is beyond the Nymphius river, subject to the Persians from of old, and had been enslaved by the Emperor Justin while still a boy, when Justin, after the capture of Amida, invaded the land of the Persians with the army of Celer. His owner, using much humanity toward him, sent him to a schoolmaster.

15.8. And at first he became secretary of Justin, and when, Anastasius having died, Justin received the kingship of the Romans, Peter, having become general, drove into love of money as no other did and used much folly toward all.

15.9. Later the Emperor Justinian sent other commanders to Lazica, and John whom they called Tzibus, a man come from obscure and inglorious origins, who had risen to a generalship for no other reason than that he was the most wicked of all men and most able to find unjust ways of money. He confounded and threw into confusion all the affairs of the Romans and Lazi.
15.10. He also persuaded the Emperor Justinian to build a city on the sea among the Lazi, Petra by name; and sitting there as in a citadel he plundered the affairs of the Lazi.

15.11. For the salt and all the other cargoes that seemed necessary to the Lazi the merchants were no longer allowed to bring to Colchis, or to buy them elsewhere thence, but he, establishing at Petra the so-called monopoly, became himself both retailer and overseer of all the business about these things, buying and selling everything to the Colchians, not as was customary, but as he was permitted.

15.12. And at the same time the barbarians were otherwise vexed that the Roman army, not wont before, was sojourning among them. Being no longer able to bear these things, they resolved to go over to the Persians and Chosroes, and at once secretly from the Romans sent envoys to them to accomplish this.

15.13. To whom it had been said that, having received pledges from Chosroes that he would never hand over the Lazi unwilling to the Romans, they should thus bring him with the Persian army into the country.

15.14. Coming, then, to the Persians and secretly to the presence of Chosroes, the envoys spoke as follows: "If ever any others in all time, having revolted in some way from their own people and gone over to wholly unknown men, Fortune, doing well, has led back beyond their hope most gladly to their former friends, consider, O greatest King,

15.15. that the Lazi are some such. For the Colchians, being allies of the Persians from the beginning, both wrought them many good things and themselves suffered; of which we have many memorials in writings, and in your palaces they are preserved to the present.
15.16. But at a later time it befell our ancestors, whether neglected by you or for some other reason (for we have nothing clear to know about these things), to become in treaty with the Romans.
15.17. And now both we and the king of Lazica give to the Persians ourselves and our land to use as you wish.

15.18. And we beg you to consider thus about us: if, having suffered no harm at the hands of the Romans, but held by ill-will, we have gone over to you, shake off at once this our supplication, thinking that the Colchians will never be faithful to you either (for the manner of friendship dissolved becomes a proof of that set up toward others after it);

15.19. but if in word friends of the Romans, but in deed having become faithful slaves, we have suffered unholy deeds from those who have tyrannized over us, receive us, your former allies, and gain as slaves those whom you used as friends, and hate a tyranny so bitter raised up near us, doing things worthy of the justice which it is ever native to the Persians to maintain.
15.20. For he who himself does no wrong is not just, unless he is also able, having it in his power, to rescue those wronged by others.

15.21. And it is worth saying some of the things the accursed Romans have dared against us. For to our king they have left only the appearance of kingship, and have taken from him the authority over deeds; and the king sits in the station of an underling, fearing the general who gives the orders.

15.22. And they have set over us a multitude of soldiery, not that they may guard the country from those who trouble it (for none of our neighbours except the Romans has troubled us), but that, shutting us up as in a prison, they may become masters of what is ours.
15.23. And reckoning to make the taking away of what is ours quicker, see, O King,

15.24. into what an idea they have come: of the provisions whatever chance to be superfluous among them, they compel the Lazi to buy against their will, and whatever Lazica is wont to bear most useful to them, these they think fit, ostensibly in word, to buy from us, the price being fixed on both sides by the purpose of the rulers.

15.25. And thus, together with the necessaries, they take all the gold from us, using the specious name of trade, but in deed forcing us as much as possible. And there is set over us a huckster ruler, who has made our want a kind of business by the authority of his office.
15.26. The cause of our revolt, then, being such, has justice on its side; and what will be expedient to you yourselves in receiving the supplication of the Lazi we will at once tell.

15.27. To the Persian realm you will add a most ancient kingdom, and you will have from it the dignity of empire extended, and it will befall you to have a share of the Roman sea through our country, in which, O King, building ships, you will reach the palace at Byzantium with no trouble. For there is no obstacle between.
15.28. And one might add that to plunder the neighbouring barbarians of the land of the Romans every year will lie in your power.
15.29. For that the land of the Lazi has till now been a bulwark to the Caucasus mountains you too, I suppose, well know.
15.30. Justice, then, leading, and advantage being present, we think it would be no good counsel not to accept these words." So much the envoys said.
15.31. And Chosroes, pleased with the words, agreed to defend the Lazi, and inquired of the envoys whether it was possible for him to go to the land of Colchis with a great army.

15.32. For from many reports, he said, he had heard before that the country was tolerably difficult of access even for an unencumbered man, being exceedingly precipitous and held together for a great extent by thick and dense trees.
15.33. But they insisted to him that the way there would be easy for the whole Persian army, cutting the trees and throwing them into the difficult ground of the precipices.
15.34. And they themselves agreed to be guides of the road and forerunners for the Persians in this work.

15.35. Lifted by this counsel, Chosroes gathered a great army and prepared the matters of the inroad, neither bringing out the plan to the Persians, except to those alone with whom he was wont to consult about secret matters, and charging the envoys to tell what was being done to no one, but he set out, ostensibly in word, for Iberia, as though to settle the affairs there; for he gave out that a Hunnic nation had attacked the Persian realm there.
16.1. Meanwhile Belisarius, being in Mesopotamia, gathered the army from all sides, and sent some to the country of the Persians on a reconnaissance.

16.2. And he himself, wishing to meet the enemy there, should they make another inroad into the land of the Romans, ordered and arranged the soldiers, who were for the most part naked and unarmed, cowering at the name of the Persians.
16.3. The scouts, returning, insisted that there would be no inroad of the enemy at present; for Chosroes had occupation with a Hunnic war elsewhere.
16.4. Belisarius, hearing this, wished at once to invade the land of the enemy with his whole army.
16.5. And Arethas came to him with a great army of Saracens, and the emperor, writing a letter, charged him to invade the enemy's land quickly.

16.6. Having called together all the commanders at Daras, he spoke as follows: "All of you, fellow-commanders, I know to be experienced in many wars, and I have gathered you at present, not that, reminding you or making some exhortation, I may urge your mind against the enemy (for I think you need no word to lead you to boldness), but that, taking some counsel among ourselves, we may rather choose what may seem best and most excellent for the emperor's affairs.
16.7. For war is wont to be set right by good counsel most of all. And those who enter into counsel must make their judgement altogether free of awe and fear.

16.8. For fear, ever astounding those who fall into it, does not allow the mind to choose the better, and awe, casting a shadow over what seem to be the better courses, carries the judgement to the opposite knowledge.
16.9. If, then, anything seems to have been resolved either by the great emperor or by me concerning the present, let this not come upon you.
16.10. For he, being far removed from what is being done,
16.11. cannot fit actions to the occasions; so that there is no fear for those who oppose him in working what will profit his affairs.
16.12. And it is impossible for me, being a man and come here after a long time from the West, not to overlook something of what is needful.
16.13. So that it befits you, awed in nothing by my judgement, to say plainly whatever shall profit ourselves and the emperor.

16.14. For from the beginning we came here, fellow-commanders, to hinder the enemy from making some inroad into our land; but now, things having turned out for us better than according to hope, it is in our power to take counsel about his.
16.15. For which, I think it just that you, having been gathered, say, hiding nothing, whatever may seem best and most expedient to each."
16.16. So much Belisarius said. And Peter and Bouzes bade him lead the army with no delay against the enemy's land. And the whole assembly at once followed their opinion.

16.17. Rhecithancus, however, and Theoctistus, the commanders of the soldiers in Lebanon, said that they too wished the same as the rest about the inroad, but feared lest, when they had left the regions of Phoenicia and Syria, Alamoundaras should plunder these at his pleasure, and the emperor be angry with them as not having guarded unravaged the country they ruled; and on this account they by no means wished to invade together with the rest of the army.

16.18. But Belisarius said that these two men by no means thought truly. For it was the time of the summer solstice. And in this season the Saracens, ever bringing for about two months an offering to their god, never use any inroad into a foreign land in this time.

16.19. Therefore, having agreed to release both of them with their followers in sixty days, he bade them too follow with the rest of the army. Belisarius, then, prepared the matters of the inroad with much haste.

17.1. Chosroes and the army of the Medes, when, having passed Iberia, they came to the borders of Lazica, the envoys leading them, cutting the trees with no one opposing—trees which, being there thick and terribly dense and high in precipitous places, made the country altogether impassable for the army—threw them into the difficult ground and wholly made the road easy.

17.2. And coming to the middle of Colchis (where the poets fable that the things about Medea and Jason took place), Gourgenes, the king of the Lazi, came and did obeisance to Chosroes the son of Cabades as master, giving over to him himself with his palaces and all Lazica.

17.3. Now Petra is a city on the sea among the Colchians, by the so-called Euxine Sea, which, being a paltry place before, the Emperor Justinian made strong by the wall and the other construction and otherwise notable.
17.4. There the Roman army, with John, learning to be, Chosroes sent an army and the general Aniabedes, as though to take them at the first shout.

17.5. But John, learning of the inroad, bade no one get outside the wall or appear to the enemy from the battlements, but arming the whole army he set it near the gates, charging them to keep silence, sending forth neither sound nor any voice.
17.6. The Persians, then, coming very near the wall, since nothing hostile was either seen or heard by them, thought the city empty of men, the Romans having left it.
17.7. Therefore they came still more about the wall, as though to set ladders straightway, since no one was defending.
17.8. And seeing and hearing nothing hostile, sending to Chosroes they declared their present situation.

17.9. And he, sending the greater part of the army, bade them make trial of the wall on all sides, and charged one of the commanders to use the ram, the engine, about the gates, while he himself, sitting on the hill which lies very near the city, became a spectator of what was done.

17.10. At once the Romans flung open the gates suddenly, and falling unexpectedly upon them destroyed most of the enemy, and especially those drawn up about the ram; the rest, with difficulty fleeing with their general, were saved.
17.11. And Chosroes, held by anger, impaled Aniabedes, as having been outgeneralled by John, a huckster and altogether unwarlike man.
17.12. But some say that not Aniabedes, but the commander who was set over those working the ram, was impaled.
17.13. And he himself, setting out with the whole army, came very near the wall of Petra and, encamping, undertook the siege.

17.14. On the next day, going around the wall, since he suspected it not very able to resist, he resolved to storm it. And leading the whole army there he set to work, and bade all shoot at the battlements.

17.15. The Romans, defending themselves, used both the engines and all arrows. At first, then, the Persians, though shooting very thickly, distressed the Romans little, and suffered much from them, being shot from above.
17.16. Then (for it was destined that Petra be taken by Chosroes) John, struck by some chance in the throat, died, and from this the other Romans came into a neglect of everything.
17.17. Then, indeed, the barbarians withdrew to the camp; for it was already growing dark. And on the next day they devised a trench to the wall in the following manner.
17.18. The city of Petra is in part inaccessible from the sea, in part from precipitous rocks which rise there on all sides; from which it has obtained this name.
17.19. It has one entrance on the level ground, and this not very broad; for extraordinary precipices hang over it on either side.

17.20. There, foreseeing this from the first, those who built the city, lest the part of the wall there be assailable for them, made long walls along each precipice of the entrance for a great extent.
17.21. And of these walls they built two towers on either side, not as was wont, but in another manner.

17.22. For they left no empty space at all in the middle of the building, but made the towers whole from the ground up to a great height with very large stones holding to one another, so that they might be least shaken by a ram or any other engine. So the wall of Petra stood.

17.23. But the Persians, secretly making a trench in the earth, got beneath one of the towers, and carrying out from there many of the stones, set in their place wood, which they burned a little later.
17.24. And the flame, rising little by little, broke through the strength of the stones, and shaking the whole tower brought it suddenly at once to the ground.
17.25. And the Romans who were in the tower perceived what was being done before only so far as not to fall together with it to the ground, but, fleeing, to get within the wall of the city.
17.26. And it was now in the power of the enemy, storming the wall on the level ground, to take the city by storm with no trouble.

17.27. Therefore the Romans, cowering, came to a parley with the barbarians, and having received pledges from Chosroes about their bodies and goods, handed over themselves and the city by agreement. Thus Chosroes took Petra.

17.28. And finding the money of John very ample, he himself took it, but of the rest neither he himself nor any of the Persians touched anything, but the Romans, holding their own, mingled with the army of the Medes.
18.1. Meanwhile Belisarius and the Roman army, having learned nothing of what was being done there, went in much good order from the city of Daras toward Nisibis.
18.2. And when they came to the middle of the road, Belisarius led the army to the right, where there were sufficient springs of water and a plain able for all to encamp.
18.3. And there he bade the camp be made, about forty-two stades from the city of Nisibis.
18.4. And all the rest marvelled greatly that he by no means wished to encamp very near the wall, and some by no means wished to follow him.

18.5. Therefore Belisarius said to those of the commanders about him as follows: "I had no wish to bring out to all what I know. For a word carried about in a camp does not know how to keep secrets, since, advancing little by little, it is brought out even to the enemy.

18.6. But seeing the most of you yielding to much disorder, and each one wishing to be himself supreme commander of the war, I shall now say among you what I ought to keep silent, having first premised this, that, with many in an army using their own self-willed judgement, it is impossible for anything needful to be done.

18.7. I think, then, that Chosroes, going against other barbarians, has by no means left his own land without a sufficient guard, especially this city, which chances to be the first and set as a bulwark of all his land.
18.8. In which I well know that he has established soldiers so great in number and so great in valour as to be able to stand in the way of our inroads. And the proof is near at hand for you.
18.9. For he has set over them Nabedes as general, who, after Chosroes himself, seems to be first among the Persians in repute and other dignity.
18.10. Whom I think will both make trial of our power, and will give us passage in no other way than being worsted by some battle at our hands.
18.11. If, then, the engagement should be very near the city, the contest will not be on equal terms for us and the Persians.
18.12. For they, coming out from the strong place and faring well, should it so chance, will take much courage to press on, and being worsted will easily escape our onset.
18.13. For the pursuit will be short for us, and the city will suffer no harm thence, which you see, I suppose, to be impregnable to those storming the wall, its soldiers defending themselves.
18.14. But if the enemy, coming here to blows with us, we conquer them, I have much hope, fellow-commanders, of taking the city.

18.15. For as the adversaries flee a long course, either, mingling with them, we shall, as is likely, burst in within the gates, or, anticipating them, we shall compel them to turn and flee to some other country, and shall make Nisibis, bereft of its defenders, easy for ourselves to take."

18.16. When Belisarius had said this, all the rest were persuaded and encamped with him and remained. But Peter, making companion of John, who commanding the troops in Mesopotamia had no paltry portion of the army, came not far from the wall, but about ten stades off, and remained quietly.

18.17. And Belisarius set those with him as for battle, and charged those under Peter to draw up as for engagement until he himself should give the signal, and to know well that the barbarians would attack them about midday, having plainly in mind that they themselves are wont to take food toward late afternoon, while the Romans take it about midday.

18.18. So Belisarius advised; but those under Peter, holding the commands of no account, about midday, distressed by the sun (for the place is tolerably parched), laid down their arms, and taking no thought of the enemy, going about in no order, ate the cucumbers growing there.
18.19. When Nabedes saw this, he led the Persian army against them at a great run.

18.20. And the Romans (for the barbarians did not escape their notice as they came out from the wall, since they were seen plainly going in the level plain) sent to Belisarius, calling him to defend them, and themselves, taking up their arms,

18.21. but held by disorder and tumult, went to meet them. And those under Belisarius, the messenger not yet having come to them, learning from the dust of the Persian inroad, came to the rescue at a run.
18.22. And the Persians, falling on, turned the Romans, who did not withstand the onset, to flight with no trouble, and pursuing destroyed fifty and seized and held the standard of Peter.
18.23. And they would have killed them all in this pursuit, seeing them look to no defence, had not Belisarius and the army with him, overtaking them, prevented it.
18.24. For the Goths, foremost of all, coming on with long and thick spears, the Persians did not withstand, but rushed to flight.
18.25. And the Romans, pursuing with the Goths, killed a hundred and fifty. For the pursuit being short, the rest got quickly within the wall.

18.26. Then, indeed, all the Romans withdrew to the camp of Belisarius, but the Persians on the following day set the standard of Peter on a certain tower instead of a trophy, and hanging sausages on it, mocked the enemy with laughter; they no longer, however, dared to come out, but guarded the city in safety.
19.1. And Belisarius, seeing Nisibis to be exceedingly strong, having no hope of taking it, hastened to go forward, that he might do the enemy some harm by a raid.
19.2. Setting out, then, with his whole army, he went forward. And having accomplished a day's journey, they came upon a fortress which the Persians call Sisauranon.
19.3. There was a multitude of inhabitants, and eight hundred horsemen, the best of the Persians, kept guard, over whom a notable man, Bleschames by name, was set.
19.4. The Romans, encamping very near the fortress, undertook a siege, and making an assault on the wall were repulsed,

19.5. having lost many in the battle. For the wall chanced to be exceedingly strong, and the barbarians most vigorously defended themselves from there against the assailants. Therefore, calling together all the commanders,

19.6. Belisarius spoke as follows: "Experience of many wars, commanders, has given us in the perplexities of affairs to foresee what shall befall, and to be able to choose the better before the dangers.
19.7. Know, then, how great an evil it is for an army to journey into a hostile land with many strongholds and many warlike men in them left behind.

19.8. Which has befallen us too at present. For as we go forward, some of the enemy following secretly from here and from the city of Nisibis will, as is likely, do us mischief in places suitable for an ambush or some other plot.

19.9. And if elsewhere another army should meet us and set itself to battle, we must of necessity draw up against both, and should thus suffer at their hands irreparable things. For I forbear to say that, stumbling in the engagement, should it so chance, we shall have no device of return to the land of the Romans for the future.

19.10. Let us not, then, using senseless haste, appear to have despoiled ourselves, nor by contentiousness harm the affairs of the Romans. For unlearned daring carries to ruin, but prudent delay is by nature ever sufficient to save those who use it.
19.11. We, then, sitting here, let us try to take this fortress, and let Arethas with his followers be sent to the regions of Assyria.
19.12. For the Saracens are by nature unable to storm walls, but most apt of all for plundering.

19.13. And some of the warlike soldiers will invade with them, that they themselves, no opposition appearing, may work irreparable things on those they fall upon, but if any hostile force should meet them, easily withdrawing they may be saved among us.

19.14. And we, having taken the fortress, if God will, then with the whole army let us cross the Tigris river, not fearing those who will do mischief behind, and knowing well how the affairs of the Assyrians stand."

19.15. Having said this, Belisarius seemed to all to speak well, and at once carried out the plan. He bade Arethas with his followers go against Assyria, and sent with them twelve hundred soldiers, of whom the most were of his own shield-bearers, setting over them two bodyguards, Trajan and John called Phagas, both good in war.

19.16. And he charged them to do everything obeying Arethas, and he bade Arethas, having plundered everything in his path, thus return to the camp and report to them what the affairs of the Assyrians were as to their power.
19.17. Those under Arethas, then, crossing the Tigris river, came into Assyria.
19.18. There, finding a good country and long unravaged, and this unguarded, plundering by a raid many of the places there, they encompassed great wealth.
19.19. Then Belisarius, having seized some of the Persians, learned that those in the fortress wanted provisions altogether.

19.20. For not, as in Daras and the city of Nisibis, are they wont to store the yearly food at public expense, but, an army of the enemy having fallen upon them unexpectedly, they had not had time to bring in any of the necessaries.
19.21. And suddenly, many having fled into the fortress, they were pressed, as is likely, by want of provisions.

19.22. Learning this, Belisarius sent George, a most intelligent man and one who shared his secrets, to make trial of the men there, whether somehow by some agreement he might be able to take the place.
19.23. And George, making an exhortation and saying much alluring to them, persuaded them, having received pledges about their safety, to hand over themselves and the fortress to the Romans.

19.24. Thus Belisarius, taking Sisauranon, released all the inhabitants, being Christians and Romans from the beginning, unharmed, but sent the Persians with Bleschames to Byzantium, and razed the wall of the fortress to the ground.
19.25. And the emperor not long after sent these Persians and Bleschames to Italy to make war on the Goths. So the affairs about the fortress of Sisauranon turned out thus.
19.26. But Arethas, fearing lest the booty be taken from him by the Romans, was no longer willing to turn back to the camp.

19.27. Sending, then, some of his followers ostensibly on a reconnaissance, he bade them, returning secretly as quickly as possible, signify to them that a great army of the enemy was about the crossing of the river.
19.28. Therefore he advised Trajan and John, going by another road, to return to the land of the Romans.
19.29. They came no longer to Belisarius, but, keeping the Euphrates river on the right, thus came to Theodosiopolis which is by the Aborrhas river.
19.30. And Belisarius and the Roman army, learning nothing about this force, were vexed, falling into a fear and suspicion neither bearable nor moderate.
19.31. And much time being spent for them in this siege, it befell many of the soldiers to be seized there by a difficult fever; for the Mesopotamia subject to the Persians is exceedingly parched.

19.32. Of which the Romans, being unaccustomed, and especially those coming from Thrace, having their dwelling in a place extraordinarily parched and in certain stifling huts in the summer season, so sickened that a third of the army lay half-dead.

19.33. The whole army, then, was eager to depart thence and to return as quickly as possible to their own land, and most of all the commanders of the troops in Lebanon, Rhecithancus and Theoctistus, seeing that the time of the Saracen offering had already passed.

19.34. Coming often to Belisarius, they begged him to release them at once, calling to witness that, having given over the regions of Lebanon and Syria to Alamoundaras, they were sitting there for no reason.
19.35. Therefore Belisarius, calling together all the commanders, set out counsel.
19.36. There rising first, John the son of Nicetas spoke as follows: "Most excellent Belisarius, I think that neither Fortune nor valour have in all time made such a general as you yourself are.
19.37. And this repute has prevailed not only among the Romans, but among all the barbarians.

19.38. This glory, however, you will most surely preserve, if you are able to bring us alive to the land of the Romans; for now our hopes are not in a fair state. For consider thus with me about this army.

19.39. The Saracens and the most warlike of the soldiers, having crossed the Tigris river, I know not how many days ago, came to such fortune that they could not even send a messenger to us; Rhecithancus and Theoctistus will depart, as you see, I suppose, very soon, thinking that the army of Alamoundaras is in the midst of Phoenicia, plundering all the places there.
19.40. And of those left, the sick are so many in number that those who would tend and convey them to the land of the Romans are far fewer than they in number.
19.41. And these things being so, if anything hostile should befall us, either remaining here or going back, no one could even report the suffering to the Romans in Daras.
19.42. For to go forward I think impossible even in word. While, then, some hope is still left, it will profit to take counsel and act for the return.
19.43. For those set in danger, especially such, not to consider their safety, but their plot against the enemy, is great folly."
19.44. So much John said, and all the rest praised it, and falling into a tumult thought fit to make the withdrawal quickly.
19.45. Therefore Belisarius, first putting the sick on the baggage animals,

19.46. led the army back. And as soon as they came to the land of the Romans, he learned all that had been done by Arethas, but was not able to take any vengeance on him, since he came no longer into his sight. So the inroad of the Romans came to this.

19.47. And to Chosroes, who had taken Petra, it was reported that Belisarius had invaded the land of Persia, and of the engagement about the city of Nisibis, and the capture of the fortress of Sisauranon, and all that the army with Arethas, having crossed the Tigris river, did.
19.48. And at once, setting a garrison in Petra, he rode off with the rest of the army and the captured Romans to the country of the Persians.
19.49. These things befell in the second inroad of Chosroes. And Belisarius, coming summoned to the emperor at Byzantium, wintered there.
20.1. At the beginning of spring Chosroes the son of Cabades for the third time invaded the land of the Romans with a great army, keeping the Euphrates river on the right.

20.2. And Candidus, the priest of Sergiopolis, when he learned that the army of the Medes had come very near, fearing for himself and the city, since at the agreed time he had by no means carried out what he had agreed with Chosroes, coming into the camp of the enemy, begged Chosroes not to be harsh with him on this account.

20.3. For he had never had money, and on this account had not even purposed at all to ransom the Surenes, but had entreated the Emperor Justinian much about these things and had been of no profit to himself.
20.4. But Chosroes held him in custody, and torturing his body most bitterly, thought fit to exact double money, as had been agreed.
20.5. And he begged him to send some men to Sergiopolis to receive all the treasures of the church there.
20.6. And when Chosroes did accordingly, Candidus sent with them one of his own followers.
20.7. The Sergiopolites, then, receiving those sent by Chosroes into the city, gave many of the treasures, insisting that nothing else was left to them.
20.8. But Chosroes said this by no means sufficed him, but thought fit to receive others more than these.
20.9. He sends, then, some ostensibly to search out exactly the money of the city, but in deed to seize the city.

20.10. And when Sergiopolis was not destined to be taken by the Persians, one of the Saracens, a Christian, ranked under Alamoundaras, Ambrus by name, coming by night to the wall of the city and reporting the whole matter, bade them by no means receive the Persians into the city.
20.11. And thus those sent by Chosroes returned to him unsuccessful, and he, seething with anger, purposed to take the city.
20.12. Sending, then, an army of about six thousand, he bade them undertake a siege and make assaults on the wall.

20.13. And they, coming there, set to work, and the Sergiopolites at first defended themselves vigorously, but then, giving up and cowering at the danger, took counsel to hand over the city to the enemy.

20.14. For they chanced to have no more than two hundred soldiers. But Ambrus, coming again to the wall by night, said that the Persians would break up the siege within two days, the water having altogether failed them.
20.15. Therefore they came to no parley at all with the enemy, and the barbarians, held by thirst, rose up and came to Chosroes. Candidus, however, Chosroes no longer released.
20.16. For it was needful, I think, that he, having disregarded what he had sworn, should be a priest no longer. So these things turned out thus.

20.17. When Chosroes came to the country of the Commageni, which they call Euphratesia, he by no means wished to turn to plunder or the capture of any place, since the things in his path as far as the Syrians he had chanced before either to take or to exact money from, as has been shown in the foregoing.

20.18. But he purposed to lead the army straight to Palestine, that he might plunder, among other things, all the treasures in Jerusalem. For he had heard by report that this country was exceedingly good and had inhabitants rich in gold.

20.19. And all the Romans, commanders and soldiers, by no means purposed to meet the enemy or to stand in the way of their passage, but, seizing the strongholds each as he could, thought it enough to guard these and themselves to be saved.

20.20. The Emperor Justinian, learning of the Persian inroad, sent Belisarius against them again. And he, riding on the public horses, which they have been accustomed to call veredi, since he had no army with him, came with much speed to Euphratesia, while Justus, the emperor's nephew, chanced to have fled to Hierapolis together with Bouzes and certain others.
20.21. And these, hearing that Belisarius had come not far off, wrote a letter to him;

20.22. and the writing declared as follows: "And now Chosroes, as you yourself know, I suppose, has made an expedition against the Romans, leading an army much larger than before, but where in the world he purposes to go is not yet clear, except that we hear he is very near, harming no place, but ever going forward by the road.
20.23. But come to us as quickly as possible, if you are able to escape the notice of the enemy's camp, that you may both be yourself safe for the emperor and may help us guard
20.24. Hierapolis." So much the writing declared. But Belisarius, not approving what was written, came to the place Europum, which is by the Euphrates river.

20.25. And from there, sending about everywhere, he gathered the army and established his camp there, and answered the commanders in Hierapolis thus: "If Chosroes is going against other men, but not subjects of the Romans, your counsel is well and most safely taken;

20.26. for those to whom it is in their power, remaining quietly, to be free of evils, it is great folly to go into some unnecessary danger; but if now this barbarian, having departed thence, shall attack some other country of the Emperor Justinian, and this an exceedingly good one, but having no garrison of soldiers, know well that to perish with valour is altogether better than to be saved without a battle.
20.27. For this would justly be called not safety, but betrayal. But come as quickly as possible to Europum, where, having gathered the whole army, I have hope, whatever God gives,
20.28. to work upon the enemy." When the commanders saw this brought to them, they took courage and left Justus with a few there to guard Hierapolis, and the rest with the army came to Europum.

21.1. And Chosroes, learning that Belisarius with the whole Roman army was encamped at Europum, no longer resolved to advance, but sent to Belisarius one of the royal secretaries, Abandanes by name, having a great repute for intelligence, to spy out what sort of man the general was, and ostensibly to complain that the Emperor Justinian had by no means sent the envoys to the Persians to dispose the matters of the peace according to the agreement. When Belisarius learned this, he did as follows.

21.2. He himself, choosing out six thousand men, tall and very fair in body, set out as though to hunt far off from the camp, and Diogenes the bodyguard and Adolius the son of Acacius, a man Armenian by race, who ever served the emperor in the palace in matters of quiet (the Romans call those on whom this honour lies silentiarii), and then commanded some Armenians, he bade cross the river with a thousand horsemen and go about the bank there, ever giving the enemy an impression that, if they should wish, having crossed the Euphrates, to go by the road to their own land, they would never permit it. And they did accordingly.

21.3. And Belisarius, when he learned that the envoy was very near, having pitched a tent of certain thick linen cloths, which they have been accustomed to call a pavilion, sat there, as in a desert place, intimating that he had come there with no preparation.
21.4. And he arranged the soldiers thus. On either side of the tent were Thracians and Illyrians, and after them Goths, and next to these Heruls, after whom were Vandals and Moors.

21.5. And they extended over a great part of the plain. For they did not stand always in the same place, but, standing apart from one another and making walks, they looked at the envoy of Chosroes carelessly and in no way earnestly.
21.6. And none of them had either cloak or any other shoulder-garment, but, clad in linen tunics and trousers, then girded up, they walked about.
21.7. And each had his horse-whip, but the weapon of one was a sword, of another an axe, of another bare bows.
21.8. And all gave an impression that, taking no thought of all else, they were eager to hunt.

21.9. Abandanes, then, coming into the presence of Belisarius, said that King Chosroes was indignant, because, as had been agreed before, the Caesar (for so the Persians call the Emperor of the Romans) had not sent the envoys to him, and on this account Chosroes had been compelled to come in arms into the land of the Romans.

21.10. But Belisarius, neither cowering, though so great a multitude of barbarians was encamped very near, nor falling into any disturbance at the word, but with a laughing and relaxed face, replies, saying, "Not in this way which Chosroes has now done is it customary for men to manage their affairs.
21.11. For all others, if anything is disputed between themselves and some of their neighbours, send embassies to them first, and when they do not obtain moderate terms, then go against them in war.
21.12. But he, getting into the midst of the Romans, then puts forward the arguments about peace." Having said so much, he dismissed the envoy.
21.13. And he, coming to Chosroes, advised him to depart as quickly as possible.

21.14. For he said he had met a general most brave and most intelligent of all men, and soldiers such as he himself had never seen, whose good order he marvelled at most of all, and that the contest was not for him and Belisarius on equal terms of danger, but it differed, that, conquering, he would conquer the Caesar's slave, but, worsted, should it so chance, he would bring great shame on his kingship and on the Persian race; and that the Romans, defeated, would easily be saved in their strongholds and their own land, but of themselves, if any reverse should befall, not even a messenger would escape to the country of the Persians.
21.15. Persuaded by this counsel, Chosroes wished to turn back to the country of the Persians, but was held by much helplessness.

21.16. For he thought the crossing of the river was being guarded by the enemy, and was not able to ride back by the same road, being altogether empty of men, since all the provisions had now failed them which they had first with them when they invaded the land of the Romans.
21.17. In the end, having reckoned much, it seemed most expedient to him, having risked a battle, to come to the land opposite, and to make the journey through a country abounding in all good things.

21.18. But Belisarius well knew that not even ten myriads of men would be sufficient to check Chosroes' crossing (for the river chances to be crossable by ships in many of the places there for a great extent, and the Persian army was otherwise mightier than to be shut off from the crossing by a few enemies); but he charged those under Diogenes and Adolius with the thousand at first to go about that bank, that they might throw the barbarian into a disturbance by some perplexity.
21.19. Whom, having frightened, as I have said, he feared lest there be some hindrance to his departing from the land of the Romans.

21.20. And it seemed to him worth much account to drive the army of Chosroes thence, having risked no battle against many myriads of barbarians with soldiers very few and simply cowering at the army of the Medes. Therefore he bade Diogenes and Adolius remain quietly.
21.21. Chosroes, then, having yoked a bridge with great speed, suddenly crossed the Euphrates river with his whole army.

21.22. For all rivers are crossable by the Persians with no trouble, since for them, going by the road, hook-shaped iron pieces are in readiness, with which, fitting long pieces of wood into one another, they improvise a bridge on the spot wherever they wish.

21.23. And as soon as he was on the bank opposite, sending to Belisarius, he said that he himself had granted to the Romans the withdrawal of the army of the Medes, but expected the envoys from them, who, it was worth saying, would be present not long after.
21.24. And Belisarius, himself too crossing the Euphrates river with the whole Roman army, at once sent men to Chosroes.

21.25. And they, when they came to him, praising the withdrawal much, promised that envoys would come to him from the emperor very soon, who would carry out toward him in deed the agreements made before concerning the peace.

21.26. And they asked to use the Romans, as friends, for their journey. And he undertook to carry this out too, if they should give him some of the men of repute as hostages on this agreement, that they would carry out the things agreed.

21.27. The envoys, then, returning to Belisarius, reported the words of Chosroes, and he, coming to Edessa, at once sent John the son of Basil, the most conspicuous of all the Edessenes in family and wealth, as a hostage to Chosroes, unwillingly.
21.28. And the Romans held Belisarius in praise, and the man seemed to them to have won more glory in this deed than when he brought Gelimer captive or Vittigis to Byzantium.

21.29. For it was truly worthy of much account and praise, when all the Romans were terrified and hiding in their strongholds, and Chosroes with a great army had got into the midst of the Roman realm, that a man, a general, with a few men, coming in the meanwhile at a swift run from Byzantium, should encamp over against the King of the Persians, and that Chosroes, unexpectedly, either fearing the fortune or the valour of the man, or deceived by certain devices, should no longer advance, but in deed flee, and in word desire the peace.

21.30. Meanwhile Chosroes, disregarding the agreements, took the city of Callinicum, no one at all defending it. For the Romans, seeing its wall rotten and altogether easy to take, ever pulling down a part of it, were renewing it with new building.

21.31. Then, indeed, having pulled down a part of it, and not yet built this remaining part, when they learned that the enemy were very near, conveying away the most precious of their goods, the well-to-do of its inhabitants withdrew to certain other strongholds, while the rest remained there without soldiers.
21.32. And a very great number of husbandmen chanced to have been gathered there. These Chosroes enslaved, and razed the whole to the ground.
21.33. And a little later, receiving the hostage John, he withdrew to his native land.

21.34. And the Armenians who had gone over to Chosroes, having received pledges from the Romans, came with Bassaces to Byzantium. These things befell the Romans in the third inroad of Chosroes, and Belisarius came summoned by the emperor to Byzantium, that he might be sent again to Italy, the affairs there being now altogether wretched for the Romans.

22.1. About these times a plague came, from which nearly all human affairs were all but extinguished. For all things that fall from heaven might perhaps have some account of cause given by daring men, such as those clever in these things love to fashion—causes by no means comprehensible to man—and to invent extravagant theories of nature, knowing well that they say nothing sound, but thinking it enough for themselves if, deceiving some of those they meet by their argument, they persuade them.
22.2. But for this evil there is no device, either to speak a pretext in word or to reckon one in thought, except indeed to refer it to God.

22.3. For it came not upon a part of the earth nor upon certain men, nor did it hold any one season of the year, whence one might be able to find sophisms of cause, but it encompassed the whole earth and harmed the lives of all men, although differing far from one another to the contrary, sparing neither nature nor age.

22.4. For whether by dwelling in places, or by manner of life, or by character of nature, or by pursuits, or by anything else by which men differ from men—in this disease alone the difference availed nothing.

22.5. And it fell upon some in summer, on others in winter, on others in the other seasons. Let, then, each say of these things as he knows, both sophist and meteorologist, but I shall go on to relate whence this disease began and in what manner it destroyed men.

22.6. It began from the Egyptians who dwell at Pelusium. And dividing in two, it went in part to Alexandria and the rest of Egypt, and in part it came to the Palestinians, neighbours of the Egyptians, and thence seized the whole earth, ever advancing by the road and walking at the fitting times.

22.7. For it seemed to go on by fixed terms and to have a fixed time of stay in each country, using the destruction carelessly toward no men, but scattering on either side to the extremities of the inhabited world, as though fearing lest some recess of the earth escape it.

22.8. For it left neither island nor cave nor mountain-top having men dwelling on it; and if it passed by any country, either not touching the men there or touching them somewhat, yet at a later time, returning there again, of the dwellers round about, on whom it had fallen most bitterly before, it touched none at all, but did not stand off from that country before it had rightly and justly rendered the measure of the dead, equal to that of those dwelling round it who had chanced to perish at the former time.
22.9. And this disease, ever beginning from the seacoast, thus went up into the inland country. And in the second year it came to Byzantium in mid-spring,

22.10. where it befell me too to be sojourning at that time. And it came about thus. Phantoms of demons in every human shape were seen by many, and those who fell in with them thought they were struck by the man they met wherever it chanced of the body, and at the same time they saw this phantom and were at once seized by the disease.

22.11. At first, then, those who fell in with them tried to turn them away, repeating the most divine of names and otherwise warding them off, each as he could, but they availed nothing at all, since the most, fleeing even into the temples, perished.

22.12. Later they no longer thought fit to give heed even to their friends calling them, but, shutting themselves up in their chambers, pretended that they did not hear, though the doors were beaten upon, fearing plainly lest it be one of the demons calling.

22.13. But to some the plague came not thus, but, seeing a vision of a dream, they thought they suffered this same thing at the hands of the one who stood over them, or heard a voice foretelling to them that they were enrolled in the number of those about to die.
22.14. But to the most, perceiving the coming thing neither waking nor in dream, it befell to be seized by the disease.
22.15. And they were seized in the following manner. They suddenly grew feverish, some roused from sleep, others walking about, others doing whatever they were doing.

22.16. And the body neither changed at all from its former colour nor was hot, as a fever having fallen on it, nor indeed did inflammation come, but the fever was so mild from the beginning until evening that it gave neither to the sick themselves nor to a physician touching them any impression of danger.

22.17. For none of those who fell into it seemed likely to die from it. But on the same day for some, on the following for others, and for others not many days later, a bubo rose, not only there where the part of the body which is below the belly is called bubo, but also within the armpit, and for some beside the ears and wherever it chanced on the thighs.

22.18. Up to this point, then, things befell nearly all alike who were seized by the disease; but from there on I cannot say whether the difference of symptoms came about in the difference of bodies, or wherever it pleased Him who brought on the disease.

22.19. For on some came a deep coma, on others a sharp delirium, and both suffered what was suited to the disease. For those on whom the coma lay, forgetting all their wonted things, seemed to sleep ever.
22.20. And if anyone tended them, they ate in the meanwhile, but some, being neglected, died at once for want of food.

22.21. But those seized by the evil of delirium were held by sleeplessness and much imagining, and suspecting that men were coming upon them to destroy them, they fell into disturbance and, crying out extraordinarily, rushed to flight.
22.22. And those who tended them, held by ceaseless toil, suffered irreparable things ever.

22.23. Therefore all pitied them no less than the suffering, not because they were pressed by the plague from approaching (for it befell neither physician nor private man to share this evil by touching the sick or the dead, since many, both ever burying or tending those who in no way belonged to them, held out in this service beyond expectation, while many, the disease falling on them without pretext, died at once), but because they were held by much hardship.

22.24. For when they fell out of their bedding and rolled on the ground, they set them back again, and they forced those who longed to throw themselves out of their dwellings, thrusting them and dragging them back.

22.25. And those by whom water chanced to be present wished to fall into it, not so much from desire of drink (for the most rushed into the sea), but the cause was most of all the disease of their minds.
22.26. And there was much toil for them about their eating too. For they did not easily take it. And many perished for want of one to tend them, either pressed by hunger,
22.27. or casting their bodies from a height. And those on whom neither coma nor delirium fell, their bubo mortified, and they, no longer holding out against the pains, died.

22.28. And one might infer that it befell all the rest in the same way, but since they were least in themselves, they were by no means able to perceive the pain, the affliction about their minds taking away their perception.

22.29. Some of the physicians, then, being at a loss through ignorance of the symptoms, and thinking that the chief of the disease was concealed in the buboes, resolved to examine the bodies of the dead. And cutting open some of the buboes, they found a terrible thing, a carbuncle grown within.
22.30. And some died at once, others many days later, and on some the body broke out in black blisters about the size of a lentil, who did not survive even one day, but all died straightway.
22.31. And many a spontaneous vomiting of blood, coming on, at once made away with.

22.32. This, however, I am able to declare, that the most approved of the physicians foretold that many would die, who a little later, beyond expectation, became free of evils, and insisted that many would be saved, who were going to perish very soon.
22.33. So there was no cause in this disease bearing on human reckoning; for to all some unreasonable outcome was for the most part borne, and the baths helped some, but harmed others no less.

22.34. And many, being neglected, died, and many beyond reason were saved. And again the matters of treatment went both ways for those who used it; and to say all, no device was found by man for safety, neither for one guarding himself beforehand not to suffer, nor for surviving when the evil had fallen, but both to suffer was without pretext and to survive was spontaneous.
22.35. And to women who were pregnant death was manifest when they were seized by the disease. For some died by miscarrying, others perished at once together with the very children they bore.
22.36. Three women in childbed, however, they say, survived though their children perished, and one, having already died in the birth, the child was both born and survived.

22.37. For those, then, on whom the bubo rose larger and came to pus, it befell to survive, being delivered of the disease, since plainly the height of the carbuncle had abated to this for them, and this was for the most part a sign of health; but those on whom the bubo remained in its former shape—on these came the evils which I just mentioned.
22.38. And to some of them it befell that the thigh withered, on which the bubo, having risen, by no means came to suppuration.
22.39. And to others it befell to survive not with the tongue whole, but to live either lisping or uttering with difficulty things unintelligible.
23.1. The disease, then, in Byzantium ran for four months, and was at its height for three most of all.

23.2. And at first there died a little more than usual, then the evil rose still more, and afterward the measure of the dead came to five thousand each day, and again to ten thousand and even more than these.
23.3. At first, then, each himself took care of the burial of the dead in his house, whom they even threw into the tombs of others, either secretly or by force; then all was confounded in all things.

23.4. For slaves remained bereft of masters, and men formerly very prosperous were deprived of the service of their household, who were either sick or dead, and many houses became altogether empty of men.
23.5. Therefore it befell some of the notable, through want, to be unburied for many days. And the care of the matter came, as is likely,

23.6. to the emperor. Distributing soldiers from the palace and money, he bade Theodorus take care of this work, who was set over the imperial responses, ever announcing to the emperor the petitions of suppliants and signifying again whatever might be the emperor's wish. The Romans call this honour referendarius in the Latin tongue.
23.7. Those, then, whose affairs at home had not yet fallen altogether into desolation, themselves each made the burials of their kin.
23.8. And Theodorus, both giving the emperor's money and spending his own besides, buried the neglected of the dead.

23.9. And when all the tombs that were before chanced to be filled with the dead, and they, digging up all the places about the city in succession and depositing there those who died each as he could, departed, and then those who made these graves, no longer holding out against the measure of the dying, went up into the towers of the wall which is in Sycae;
23.10. and taking off the roofs they threw the bodies there in no order, and heaping them up, each as it chanced, and filling them with the dead, so to speak, all of them,

23.11. then covered them again with the roofs. And from this an ill-smelling vapour, going into the city, distressed the men there still more, especially if some wind blowing favourably from there should breathe upon them.

23.12. And all the customs about burials were then overlooked. For neither were the dead carried escorted as was customary, nor sung over as was wont, but it was enough if someone, carrying one of the dead on his shoulders and coming to the parts of the city by the sea, threw him there, where, thrown into the boats in heaps, they were to be conveyed wherever it chanced.

23.13. Then too those of the populace who before had been partisans, laying aside their hatred toward one another, took care in common of the holy rites of the dead, and themselves carrying and burying the dead who did not belong to them.

23.14. But also those who before, standing by base and wicked deeds, rejoiced in them, these, shaking off their lawlessness in life, exactly practised piety, not having learned prudence nor having become lovers of virtue suddenly;

23.15. since for men whatever is fixed by nature or by long teaching is impossible to be changed so easily, unless some divine good breathed upon them; but then nearly all, struck by what befell, and thinking they would die very soon, by all necessity, as is likely, learned moderation for the occasion.

23.16. And so, as soon as they were delivered of the disease and saved and supposed they were now in safety, the evil having gone over to certain other men, they made a quick change of mind for the worse, and displayed the perversity of their practices more than before, conquering themselves most of all in wickedness and other lawlessness; since one would not say what is false in insisting that this disease, whether by some chance or by providence, having exactly selected the most wicked, let them go. But these things have been shown at a later time.
23.17. Then it did not seem easy to see anyone marketing in Byzantium, but all who chanced to be sound in body, sitting at home, either tended the sick or mourned the dead.

23.18. And if one was able to meet anyone going about, this man was carrying one of the dead. And all work ceased, and the craftsmen let go all their crafts, and all other works which each had in hand.

23.19. In a city, then, simply abounding in all good things, an exact famine reigned. To have bread or anything else in plenty seemed difficult and worth much account; so that for some of the sick it seemed to befall that the end of their life came untimely for want of necessaries.

23.20. And to say all, it was not possible to see anyone in Byzantium at all clad in a cloak, especially when the emperor chanced to be sick (for it befell him too that a bubo rose), but in a city holding the kingship of the whole Roman realm all, clad in garments in the manner of private men, remained quietly.
23.21. The matters of the plague, then, both in the rest of the land of the Romans and in Byzantium, stood thus. And it fell also upon the land of the Persians and upon all the other barbarians.
24.1. Chosroes chanced to have come from the Assyrians to a place of the Adarbiganians toward the north wind, whence he purposed to invade the Roman realm through Persarmenia.

24.2. The great fire-temple is there, which the Persians worship most of all the gods. There the Magi, guarding the fire unquenchable, both perform all other rites exactly and use an oracle for the greatest of matters. This is the fire which the Romans in former times called Hestia and worshipped.
24.3. There one sent from Byzantium to Chosroes reported that Constantianus and Sergius would come to him as envoys for the agreement very soon.
24.4. These two men were both orators and exceedingly intelligent, Constantianus an Illyrian by race, and Sergius from the city of Edessa, which is in Mesopotamia.
24.5. Awaiting whom Chosroes remained quietly. And in this journey, Constantianus having fallen sick and much time being spent, it befell that the plague fell upon the Persians.

24.6. Therefore Nabedes, then holding the generalship in Persarmenia, by the king's command sent the priest of the Christians in Doubios to Valerian, the general in Armenia, to charge with the slowness of the envoys and to urge the Romans toward the peace with all eagerness.

24.7. And he, coming with his brother to the Armenians and meeting Valerian, insisted that he himself, as a Christian, was well-disposed toward the Romans, and that King Chosroes was ever persuaded by him in all counsel; so that if the envoys of the Romans came with him to the country of the Persians, there would be no hindrance to disposing the peace as they wished.

24.8. So much the priest said; and the priest's brother, meeting Valerian secretly, said that Chosroes was in great evils. For his son, setting himself to a tyranny, had risen against him, and he himself, together with all the Persian army, was seized by the disease; therefore he now wished to come to the agreement with the Romans.

24.9. When Valerian heard this, he at once dismissed the bishop, promising that the envoys would come to Chosroes not long after, and himself referred the words which he had heard to the Emperor Justinian.

24.10. By which the emperor, at once moved, charged both him and Martin and the other commanders to invade the enemy's land as quickly as possible. For he knew well that none of the enemy would stand in their way.

24.11. And he bade them, all gathered into one, thus make the inroad against the Persarmenians. When the commanders saw this letter brought to them, all together with their followers streamed to the regions of Armenia.

24.12. And already Chosroes a little before, for fear of the disease leaving Adarbiganon, had gone off with the whole army to Assyria, where the suffering of the plague had not yet come. Valerian, then, encamped very near Theodosiopolis with the troops about him, and Narses ranged himself with him, having Armenians and some of the Heruls with him.

24.13. And Martin the general of the East, with Ildiger and Theoctistus, coming to the fortress of Citharizon, and pitching his camp there, remained; this fortress is distant a journey of four days from Theodosiopolis; where Peter too came not long after with Adolius and certain other commanders.
24.14. And Isaaces the brother of Narses led the troops there. And Philemuth and Verus came with the Heruls following them to the regions of Chorzianene, not far from the camp of Martin.

24.15. And Justus the emperor's nephew and Peranius and John the son of Nicetas, with Domnentiolus and John surnamed Phagas, encamped by the fortress called Phison, which is very near the borders of Martyropolis.
24.16. Thus, then, the Roman commanders encamped with their followers, and the whole army came together to thirty thousand.
24.17. All these neither were gathered into one, nor indeed came to a parley with one another. But the generals, sending to one another some of their followers, inquired about the inroad.

24.18. But suddenly Peter, having consulted no one, with his men inconsiderately invaded the enemy's land. When Philemuth and Verus, the leaders of the Heruls, learned this on the following day, they at once followed.
24.19. And when those under Martin and Valerian learned these things, they used the inroad quickly.

24.20. And all mingled with one another a little later in the enemy's land, except Justus and those with him, who, being encamped far off, as has been said, from the rest of the army, and learning of their inroad later in time, themselves too invaded as quickly as possible the enemy's land over against them, but by no means were able to mingle with their fellow-commanders.
24.21. All the rest together advanced straight to Doubios, neither plundering nor doing any other unkindness to the country of the Persians.
25.1. Now Doubios is a country good in other respects and having a sufficient healthiness of air and waters, distant a journey of eight days from Theodosiopolis.
25.2. And there are plains fit for horsemen there, and many very populous villages are settled very near one another, and many merchants for business dwell in them.

25.3. For from the Indians and the neighbouring Iberians and nearly all, so to speak, the nations among the Persians, and some of the Romans, bringing in their cargoes they trade with one another there.
25.4. And the priest of the Christians they call Catholicos in the Greek tongue, because he, being one, is set over all the places there.

25.5. And about a hundred and twenty stades from Doubios, on the right as one goes from the land of the Romans, is a mountain difficult of access and otherwise precipitous, and a certain village lying in a very narrow difficult ground, Anglon by name.
25.6. There Nabedes, as soon as he learned of the inroad of the enemy, withdrawing with his whole army and taking courage in the strength of the place, shut himself up.
25.7. And the village lies at the extremities of the mountain, and a strong fortress, of the same name as this village, is in the precipitous ground.
25.8. Nabedes, then, having blocked the entrances to the village with stones and wagons, made it still more difficult of access.

25.9. And in front, having dug a certain ditch, he stationed his army there, having set in ambush in certain old little houses ambushes of foot. The whole Persian army came together to about four thousand men.

25.10. These things, then, were being done thus. But the Romans, coming to a place distant a day's journey from Anglon, and seizing one of the enemy who was going on a reconnaissance, inquired where in the world Nabedes now was. And he said that the man had withdrawn from Anglon with the whole army of the Medes.
25.11. When Narses heard this he was indignant, and reviled his fellow-commanders, reproaching them with the delay.
25.12. And this same thing others too did, insulting one another, and for the rest, taking no thought of battle or danger, were eager to plunder the places there.

25.13. Setting out, then, without a general and without order, in no array they went forward, neither having any watchword among themselves, as is customary in such contests, nor distinguished anywhere in rank.
25.14. For the soldiers, mingling with the baggage-carriers, journeyed as though going to a ready plunder of great wealth.
25.15. But when they came near Anglon, they sent scouts, who, returning to them, reported the array of the enemy.

25.16. And the generals, struck with consternation at the unexpectedness, thought it shameful and altogether unmanly to turn back with so great an army in number, but, arranging as best they could from the present, divided the army into three corps and went straight against the enemy.

25.17. Peter, then, held the right wing, Valerian the left, and into the centre those under Martin were arranged. And coming very near the adversaries they remained quiet, keeping their order with disorder.
25.18. The cause was both the difficult ground, being exceedingly precipitous, and that, arranged on the spur of the moment, they set themselves to the battle.

25.19. And besides, the barbarians, drawing themselves into a small space, remained quietly, looking about at the power of the adversaries, it having been told them by Nabedes by no means to begin the fight, but, if the enemy should attack anywhere, to defend themselves as far as possible.
