25.20. And first Narses with the Heruls and the Romans following him came to blows with the enemy, and a push having arisen he routed the Persians over against him.
25.21. And the barbarians, fleeing, went up to the fortress at a run, where they wrought irreparable deeds upon one another in the narrowness.
25.22. And then Narses himself, urging on those about him, pressed the enemy still more,

25.23. and the rest of the Romans set to work. But coming out suddenly from the little houses along the narrows, those who lay in ambush, as has been said, killed some of the Heruls, falling on them unexpectedly, and struck Narses himself on the temple.
25.24. And Isaaces his brother, when he was mortally struck, led him out of the fighting. And he died a little later, having proved a brave man in this toil.
25.25. And much disturbance, as is likely, from this falling upon the Roman army, Nabedes let loose his whole Persian army against the adversaries.

25.26. And they, shooting in the narrows into a very great multitude of enemies, both killed many others easily and especially the Heruls, who, having first fallen upon the adversaries with Narses, fought for the most part unguarded.
25.27. For the Heruls have neither helmet nor corselet nor any other safeguard, except a shield and a thick cloak, which, girt up, they set themselves to the contest.

25.28. The slave Heruls, indeed, go to battle even without a shield, and when they become brave men in war, then their masters allow them shields to hold before them in the engagements. So the affairs of the Heruls stand thus.
25.29. And the Romans, not enduring the enemy, all fled at full force, neither remembering valour nor having any shame or other good thing in mind.

25.30. But the Persians, suspecting that they had not turned to so shameful a flight, but were using some ambushes against them, pursued as far as the difficult ground and then turned back, not daring to fight in the open, few against many.

25.31. The Romans, however, and especially all the generals, thinking that the enemy were ever making a pursuit against them, fled still more, letting slip no opportunity, urging on their running horses with whip and shout, and throwing their corselets and their other arms to the ground with haste and tumult.

25.32. For they had no courage to take their stand and array against the Persians who were overtaking them, but had the hopes of safety in the feet of their horses alone; and, to say all, the flight became such that scarcely one of their horses survived for them, but when they stopped running, falling at once they perished.
25.33. And this was a great disaster for the Romans, such as never before befell. For many of them died, and still more came under the enemy.
25.34. And their arms and baggage animals the enemy took so great in number that the affairs of the Persians seemed to become richer from this deed.

25.35. And Adolius, passing through a fortress in this retreat lying in Persarmenia, was struck on the head with a stone by one of the inhabitants there and perished; and those under Justus and Peranius, having invaded the regions of Tarauna and plundered a few things, at once returned.
26.1. In the following year Chosroes the son of Cabades for the fourth time invaded the land of the Romans, leading the army against Mesopotamia.
26.2. This inroad of this Chosroes was made not against the Emperor Justinian, nor against any other of men, but only against the God whom the Christians worship.
26.3. For when, in the first onset, having failed of Edessa, he withdrew, much dejection had come upon him and the Magi, as having been worsted by the God of the Christians.
26.4. Consoling which, Chosroes threatened in his palaces to enslave all the Edessenes to the country of the Persians and to make the city a pasture for sheep.

26.5. With his whole army, then, coming near Edessa, he sent some of the Huns who followed him against the wall of the city which is above the hippodrome, to do no other mischief, but to seize the flocks which the shepherds chanced to have stationed in great number there by the wall, taking courage in the strength of the place, because it was exceedingly steep, and thinking the enemy would never dare to go so near the wall.
26.6. The barbarians, then, were already laying hold of the flocks, but the shepherds most vigorously prevented them.

26.7. And many Persians having come to the aid of the Huns, the barbarians were able to take off some herd from there, but, the Roman soldiers and some of the populace having come out against the enemy, the battle became hand to hand, and the herd returned of its own accord to the shepherds.
26.8. And one of the Huns, fighting before the rest, troubled the Romans most of all.
26.9. And some husbandman, hitting him with a sling on the right knee, struck him, and he fell prone at once from his horse to the ground, which encouraged the Romans still more.
26.10. And the battle, having begun in the morning, ended at midday, in which both sides, thinking they had the upper hand, parted.
26.11. And the Romans got within the wall, but the barbarians all encamped, bivouacking seven stades from the city.
26.12. Then Chosroes either saw some vision of a dream or some thought came to him, that, having attempted twice, if he should be unable to take Edessa, it would befall him to take on much shame.
26.13. Therefore he resolved to sell the withdrawal to the Edessenes for much money.
26.14. On the following day, then, Paul the interpreter, coming to the wall, said that the Romans ought to send some of the men of repute to Chosroes.
26.15. And they quickly choosing out four of the conspicuous among themselves sent them.

26.16. When these came to the camp of the Medes, Zabergan, meeting them by the king's purpose and frightening them with many threats, inquired of them which of the two was more to be chosen, the things leading to peace or to war.
26.17. And when they agreed that they would choose peace before dangers, "Then," said Zabergan, "you must buy this for much money."
26.18. And the envoys said they would give as much as they had given before, when, having taken Antioch, he came against them.
26.19. And Zabergan dismissed them with laughter, that, having deliberated most continually about their safety, they might thus come to them again.

26.20. And a little later Chosroes, sending for them, when they came to him, recounted both how many and in what manner he had enslaved Roman places, and threatened that more dreadful things would befall the Edessenes at the hands of the Persians, unless they gave him all the money they had within the wall; for thus alone would the army depart thence, he said.

26.21. The envoys, hearing this, agreed to buy peace from Chosroes, if he should not enjoin upon them the impossible; but the end of the danger, they said, was clear to none of all before the contest.
26.22. For war for those who wage it is never on the agreed terms. Then, indeed, with anger Chosroes bade the envoys depart as quickly as possible.

26.23. On the eighth day from the siege, wishing to raise an artificial mound against the wall of the city, since he had cut the trees with their very leaves from places somewhere near and set them in a square before the wall, where an arrow from the city could not reach, and heaping a great quantity of earth above the trees, he threw on a great mass of stones, not suited for building, but cut at random, caring only for this, that the mound might rise to a great height as quickly as possible.
26.24. And ever throwing in long pieces of wood between the earth and the stones, he made a binding of the work,

26.25. lest, having become high, it be weak. But Peter the Roman general (for he chanced to be there with Martin and Peranius), wishing to check those who were doing this, sent some of the Huns who followed him against them.
26.26. And they, coming suddenly, killed many, and most of all one of the bodyguards, Argek by name;
26.27. for he alone killed twenty-seven. But the barbarians for the rest keeping exact guard, no one could come out against them any longer.

26.28. And when the craftsmen of this work, advancing, came within bowshot, the Romans, now defending themselves most vigorously from the wall, plied both the slings and the bows against them. Therefore the barbarians devised the following.

26.29. Coverings of goat's hair, which they call Cilician cloths, having sufficient thickness and length, hanging them from long pieces of wood, they ever set in front of those working the agesta (for so the Romans called what was being done in the Latin tongue).
26.30. For there neither fire-bearing arrows nor the other missiles could reach, but, being repelled there upon the coverings, all remained.

26.31. And then the Romans, fallen into great fear, sent the envoys to Chosroes with much tumult, and Stephanus with them, learned among the physicians of his time, who, having once cured Cabades the son of Perozes when sick, had become master of great wealth from him.
26.32. He, when he came with the others to Chosroes, spoke as follows: "All from of old have held the humanity of a king to be the mark of a good one.
26.33. Then, O most mighty King, to you working slaughters and battles and enslavements of cities, it will perhaps be possible to obtain other names, but to seem to be good will never be.
26.34. And yet least of all ought anything paltry to befall the city of the Edessenes from you.

26.35. For from there I have come, who, foreseeing nothing of what was to be, reared you and became a counsellor to your father, that he should set you up as successor to his rule, and so became most to blame for the kingship of the Persians to you, and for the present evils to my fatherland.
26.36. For men for the most part fasten on themselves most of the misfortunes of what shall come.
26.37. But if any memory of such a benefit comes upon you, do us no further harm, giving me this recompense, from which, O King, it will befall you not to seem most savage." So much Stephanus said.
26.38. But Chosroes agreed that he would not depart thence before the Romans handed over to him both Peter and Peranius, because they, being his ancestral slaves, had dared to oppose him.

26.39. And if this were not pleasing for the Romans to do, but they were forced to choose one of two things, either to give him five hundred centenaria of gold, or to receive into the city some of his intimates, who, having searched out all the money, would come to him bringing all the gold and silver that chanced to be there,

26.40. but would leave the rest to the owners to have. These things Chosroes hurled out, having hope of taking Edessa with no trouble. And the envoys (for all that he announced seemed impossible to them), perplexed and exceedingly distressed, walked to the city.
26.41. And when, getting within the wall, they reported the things from Chosroes, the city became full of tumult and lamentations.
26.42. The construction of the mound, then, both rose to a great height and went forward with much haste. And the Romans, not knowing what to do, again sent the envoys to Chosroes.

26.43. And they, when they came to the camp of the enemy, saying they had come to beg about the same things, obtained no speech at all from the Persians, but, driven thence with insult and much tumult, went to the city.

26.44. At first, then, the Romans attempted to overtop the wall facing the mound with another building; but when this too the work of the Persians far surpassed already, they stood off from the building, and persuaded Martin to arrange the matters about the agreement in whatever way he wished. And he, coming very near the camp of the enemy, came to a parley with some of the commanders among the Persians.

26.45. And they, deceiving Martin, said that their king wished peace, but that he himself was by no means able to persuade the Emperor of the Romans, leaving off his contentiousness against Chosroes, ever to make peace with him;

26.46. since even Belisarius—who, that he far surpassed Martin in power and dignity not even he himself would deny—had lately persuaded the King of the Persians, who was indeed in the midst of the Romans, to depart thence to the country of the Persians, promising that envoys would come to him not long after from Byzantium and confirm the peace in security, but had done none of what was agreed, having been unable to force the judgement of the Emperor Justinian.

27.1. Meanwhile the Romans did as follows. Having made a trench from the city beneath the mound of the enemy, they bade those digging not let go of this work, until they should get under the middle of the mound. For there they purposed to burn this mound.
27.2. And the trench advancing about the middle of the mound, a certain noise came to the Persians standing above.
27.3. And perceiving what was being done, they themselves, beginning from above on either side of the middle, dug, so that they might catch the Romans doing mischief there.

27.4. When the Romans learned this, they refrained from it, throwing earth on the emptied space, but from the extremity of the mound below, which chanced to be by the wall, carrying out wood and stones and earth, they made as it were the shape of a little house, and threw in there dry stumps of the most easily burning trees, soaked in oil made of cedar and in much sulphur and pitch.

27.5. And they had these things in readiness, but the commanders of the Persians, often meeting Martin, discoursed such things as I have said, giving an impression that they would accept the arguments about peace.

27.6. But when the mound was now finished for them, and, approaching the wall of the city, rose high overtopping it greatly, they dismissed Martin, expressly refusing the agreement, and were about to set to work for the rest.

27.7. Therefore the Romans at once burned the stumps of the trees which had been prepared for this. And the fire having burned a part of the mound, but not yet been able to reach through the whole, it chanced that all the wood was consumed. For they ever threw other wood into the trench, letting slip no opportunity.

27.8. And the fire now working through the whole mound, a smoke appeared above everywhere on the mound by night, and the Romans, not yet wishing to give the Persians perception of what was being done, devised the following.

27.9. Filling small vessels with coals and fire, they sent these and fire-bearing arrows thickly everywhere over the mound; which the Persians, who had guard there, going about with all haste, extinguished, and thought that from this the smoke arose.
27.10. And as the evil advanced, the barbarians came to the rescue in great multitude, but the Romans, shooting at them from the wall, killed many.
27.11. There Chosroes too came about sunrise, and the greater part of the army followed him, and going up onto the mound he first got perception of the evil.
27.12. For he declared that the cause of the smoke was below, not from what the enemy were shooting, and bade the whole army come to the rescue quickly.

27.13. And the Romans, taking courage, insulted them, while of the barbarians some, throwing on earth, others water, where the smoke showed through, hoped to get the better of the danger, but were able to accomplish nothing at all.

27.14. For where the earth was thrown on, there the smoke, as is likely, was checked, but elsewhere not long after it gave out, the fire compelling itself to force its exit where it could; and the water, where it most fell, made the pitch and the sulphur work much more and brought the material in its path to a height, and ever led the fire forward, since within the mound it was by no means able to reach with so much water as to be able to quench the flame by excess.
27.15. And the smoke toward late afternoon became so great that it was manifest both to the Carrhenes and to certain others dwelling far beyond.
27.16. And many Persians and Romans having gone up over the mound, and a battle and push having arisen there, the Romans conquered.
27.17. Then too the flame, brilliantly given out, appeared above the mound, and the Persians refrained from this work.
27.18. On the sixth day from this, at deep dawn, with ladders they secretly assaulted a portion of the wall where the fortress is named.
27.19. And the Romans who had guard there sleeping a gentle sleep, since the night was going to its end, they quietly set the ladders against the wall and were already climbing up.
27.20. But one of the husbandmen, alone awake among all the Romans, with shouting and much tumult roused them all.
27.21. And a fierce battle having arisen, the Persians were worsted, and withdrew to the camp, leaving there the ladders, which the Romans drew up at their pleasure.
27.22. And Chosroes about midday sent a great portion of the army against the so-called great gate as though to storm the wall.
27.23. Whom the Romans, meeting—not soldiers only, but also husbandmen and some of the populace—and conquering in battle, routed the barbarians by far.
27.24. And the Persians being still pursued, Paul the interpreter, coming from Chosroes, reported among the Romans that Rhecinarius had come from Byzantium for the peace, and thus both sides parted.
27.25. Already some days before Rhecinarius had come to the camp of the barbarians.

27.26. But the Persians by no means brought this out to the Romans, plainly awaiting the plot against the wall, that, if they should be able to take it, they might seem in no way to transgress against the treaties, but, worsted, which happened, they might make the terms of the agreement, the Romans inviting them to it.

27.27. When Rhecinarius got within the gates, the Persians thought fit that those who would dispose the peace should go to Chosroes very soon, but the Romans said that envoys would be sent three days later; for now Martin the general was badly affected in body.

27.28. And Chosroes, suspecting that the word was not sound, prepared the matters of battle. And then he threw a very great quantity of bricks onto the mound, and two days later went against the wall of the city with his whole army as though to storm it.
27.29. And setting at each gate some of the commanders and a portion of the army, and surrounding the whole wall thus, he brought up ladders and engines against it.
27.30. And behind he arranged all the Saracens with some of the Persians, not that they should assault the wall, but that, the city being taken, they themselves might net and seize the fugitives.
27.31. With such a purpose Chosroes thus arranged the army. And the battle, having begun in the morning, at first the affairs of the Persians had the upper hand.
27.32. For many fought against very few, since most of the Romans were unaware of what was being done and altogether unprepared.
27.33. But as the engagement advanced, the city became full of tumult and disturbance, and all now, with the very women and little children, went up onto the wall.
27.34. Those in their prime, then, with the soldiers, defended themselves against the enemy most vigorously, and many of the husbandmen displayed marvellous deeds against the barbarians.
27.35. And children and women with the aged gathered stones for the fighters and rendered other service.

27.36. And some, filling many cauldrons with oil and heating them everywhere on the wall for a sufficient time and pouring the oil, exceedingly boiling, with certain sprinklers, distressed still more the enemy who approached the wall.
27.37. And the Persians now, giving up, threw down their arms, and coming into the king's sight said they were no longer able to hold out against the toil.
27.38. But Chosroes, held by much anger and urging all on with threats, drove them against the enemy.
27.39. And they with shouting and much tumult brought up the towers and the other engines to the wall and set on the ladders, as though to take the city at the first shout.
27.40. But the Romans shooting thickly and defending themselves with all might, the barbarians were routed by force, and the Romans mocked Chosroes as he withdrew, inviting him to storm the wall.
27.41. Only Azarethes about the gates called the Soenae fought with his followers, where they call the place Tripyrgia.

27.42. And the Romans there not being a match for them, but giving up against the assaults, the barbarians, having now broken through the outer wall, which they call the outwork, in many places, pressed most vigorously on those who defended themselves from the great wall, until Peranius with many soldiers and some of the Edessenes came out against them and, conquering in battle, drove them off.

27.43. And the storming of the wall, having begun in the morning, ended toward late afternoon, and both sides remained quietly that night, the Persians fearing for their palisades and for themselves, and the Romans gathering stones onto the battlements and making all other preparation, as though to fight on the morrow with the enemy when they should assault the wall.

27.44. On the following day, then, none of the barbarians came to the wall, but on the day after, a portion of the army, Chosroes urging them on, assaulted the gates called Barlaus, but the Romans meeting them, they were worsted by far in the battle and in a short time withdrew to the camp.
27.45. And then Paul the Persian interpreter, coming to the wall, called Martin, that he might dispose the matters of the agreement.

27.46. And thus, Martin having come to a parley with the commanders of the Persians, they came to terms, and Chosroes, having received five centenaria from the Edessenes, left them in writing the agreement to do the Romans no further harm, and burning all the palisades withdrew home with his whole army.

28.1. About this time two generals of the Romans died, Justus the emperor's nephew and Peranius the Iberian, Justus destroyed by disease, but it befell Peranius, having fallen from his horse in a hunt, to be burst.

28.2. Therefore the emperor, setting up others in their place, sent Marcellus, his own nephew just becoming bearded, and Constantianus, who a little before had been sent together with Sergius as envoy to Chosroes.
28.3. Then the Emperor Justinian sent envoys to Chosroes for the agreement, Constantianus and Sergius.
28.4. And they overtake him in Assyria, where there are two towns, Seleucia and Ctesiphon, built by the Macedonians who, after Alexander the son of Philip, ruled the Persians and the nations there.
28.5. And the Tigris river divides both these; for they have no other country between.
28.6. There the envoys, meeting Chosroes, thought fit that he give back the places of Lazica to the Romans and confirm with them most firmly the matters of the peace.

28.7. But Chosroes said it was not easy for them to come to terms with one another, unless, having first made some armistice, and thus ever going more fearlessly to one another, they should both dissolve their differences and establish the matters of the peace in security for the rest.
28.8. And he said that for the perpetual armistice the Emperor of the Romans must both give him money and send a certain physician, Tribunus by name, that he should pass a fixed time with him.
28.9. For this physician chanced to have rid him of a grievous disease before, and from this was his friend and most longed-for.
28.10. When the Emperor Justinian heard this, he at once sent Tribunus and the money, amounting to twenty centenaria.
28.11. And thus a treaty was made for the Romans and the Persians for five years, in the nineteenth year of the Emperor Justinian holding the supreme rule.
28.12. A little later Arethas and Alamoundaras, the rulers of the Saracens, waged war against one another by themselves, neither the Romans nor the Persians helping them.

28.13. And Alamoundaras, taking by a raid one of the sons of Arethas who was pasturing horses, at once sacrificed him to Aphrodite, and from this it was known that Arethas was not betraying the affairs of the Romans to the Persians.

28.14. After this both came to battle with their whole army, and those with Arethas conquered by force, and routing the enemy killed many. And Arethas came near to taking two of the sons of Alamoundaras alive, but did not take them. So the affairs of the Saracens stood thus.

28.15. But Chosroes, the King of the Persians, became manifest as having made the armistice with the Romans with a treacherous mind, that, taking them slack on account of the peace, he might work some irreparable thing.

28.16. For in the third year of the armistice he contrived as follows. There were among the Persians two brothers, Phabrizus and Isdigousnas, invested there with the greatest offices and otherwise the most wicked in reckoning of all the Persians, and having great repute for cleverness and ill-disposition.

28.17. Having purposed, then, to take the city of Daras by a raid and to drive all the Colchians out of Lazica, and to settle Persians as inhabitants in their place, he chose these two men to serve in both works;

28.18. for it seemed a windfall and worth much account to him, having appropriated the land of Colchis, to hold it in security of possession, reckoning that this would be expedient to the Persian realm in many ways.
28.19. For he would have Iberia in safety for the future, the Iberians no longer having any men to whom, having revolted, they might be saved;

28.20. for when the most notable of these barbarians together with Gourgenes the king resolved on revolt, as I have said before, the Persians neither conceded that a king should be set up for them for the future, nor were the Iberians of their own will subject to the Persians, but were held by much suspicion and distrust toward one another.
28.21. And the Iberians were manifestly most exceedingly indignant and would revolt not long after, if ever they should be able to take hold of some opportunity.

28.22. And by the Huns dwelling near Lazica the Persian realm would for ever be unravaged, and they could send them more easily and with less toil against the Roman realm, whenever it should be his wish; for the land of the Lazi is nothing else to the barbarians dwelling in the Caucasus than a bulwark.

28.23. And most of all in this he hoped the mastery of Lazica would profit the Persians, that, setting out from it, they would be able, with no trouble, overrunning by foot and by ships the places on the so-called Euxine Sea, to subdue the Cappadocians and the Galatians and Bithynians adjoining them, and to take Byzantium by a raid, no one opposing them.
28.24. For these reasons, then, Chosroes wished to appropriate Lazica, but he had no confidence at all toward the Lazi.

28.25. For when the Romans withdrew from Lazica, the multitude of the Lazi was tolerably vexed with the Persian realm. For the Persians are, if any others, of a solitary disposition and exceedingly hard in their way of life.

28.26. And their laws are difficult of approach for all men, and their commands by no means bearable. But toward the Lazi especially the difference both of disposition and of way of life appears great, since the Lazi are Christians most of all, but with the Persians all things concerning the divine are the opposite of theirs.
28.27. And apart from these things, salt is in no way produced in Lazica, nor indeed does grain or wine or any other good thing grow.

28.28. But from the Romans of the seacoast all things come in to them by ships, and these not giving gold to those who deal with them, but skins and slaves and whatever else chances to be there in great surplus.

28.29. Of which, as is likely, being shut off for the rest, they were distressed. When Chosroes perceived this, he was eager to anticipate in safety, before they should make any revolution against him.

28.30. And in his deliberation it seemed most expedient to him, having made away with Gubazes the king of the Lazi as quickly as possible, to remove the Lazi thence with all their people, and thus to settle Persians and certain other nations in this country.

28.31. Having resolved these things, Chosroes sends Isdigousnas as though on an embassy ostensibly in word to Byzantium, and sent with him five hundred Persians, chosen for valour, charging them to get into the city of Daras and to lodge in many houses, and to burn all these by night, and, the Romans being occupied about this fire, as is likely, all of them, to open the gates at once and receive into the city the rest of the Persian army.

28.32. For it had been said before to the commander of the city of Nisibis to have a multitude of soldiers in readiness, hiding very near. For thus Chosroes thought they would with no trouble both make away with all the Romans and, having seized the city of Daras securely, hold it.

28.33. But someone well knowing what was being done, a Roman man, who had a little before come as a deserter to the Persians, tells the whole matter to George, who then had his abode there, whom I have mentioned in the foregoing, as having persuaded the Persians besieged in the fortress of Sisauranon to hand over themselves to the Romans.

28.34. George, then, meeting this envoy at the borders of the Romans and Persians, said that what was being done was not according to embassy, and that never should so great a multitude of Persians lodge in a Roman city.
28.35. For all the rest must be left in the place Ammodios, and he himself, with a few, might enter the city of Daras.
28.36. Isdigousnas, then, was indignant and seemed distressed, as having been needlessly outraged, although sent on an embassy to the Emperor of the Romans.
28.37. But George, paying no heed to him in his savagery, saved the city for the Romans. For with twenty men only he received Isdigousnas into the city.

28.38. Having failed of this attempt, then, this barbarian came to Byzantium as though on an embassy, bringing with him his wife and two daughters (for this was for him the screen of the throng that had come together), and coming into the emperor's sight he was able to say nothing great or small about any serious matter, although he spent not less than ten months in the land of the Romans.

28.39. The gifts, however, from Chosroes, as is customary, and a letter he gave to the emperor, through which Chosroes thought fit that the Emperor Justinian should signify whether his body was in the best state of health.
28.40. This Isdigousnas, however, the Emperor Justinian saw with much friendliness, most of all the envoys we know, and held him in sufficient honour;
28.41. so that even when he feasted him, Braducius, who followed him as interpreter, he reclined with him on the couch, a thing that had never happened before in all time.
28.42. For no one ever saw an interpreter even of any of the lesser rulers, much less one made table-companion to a king.
28.43. But also more magnificently than befits an envoy he received and dismissed this man, although he had made the embassy for no purpose,

28.44. as I have said. For if one should reckon up the expenses and the gifts which Isdigousnas, departing, took thence, he will find them amounting to more than ten centenaria of gold. So the matter of the plot against the city of Daras came to this for Chosroes.

29.1. And to Lazica first he sent a great quantity of wood suitable for the making of ships, telling no one for what purpose he sent it, but in word he sent these to set up engines about the wall of Petra.

29.2. Then choosing out three hundred warlike Persians and setting over them Phabrizus, whom I just mentioned, he sends them there, whom he charged to make away with Gubazes as secretly as possible; for the rest he would take care of himself.

29.3. This wood, then, when it was conveyed to Lazica, chanced to be struck by lightning suddenly and reduced to ashes; and Phabrizus, coming with the three hundred to Lazica, set about how he might carry out concerning Gubazes the things enjoined by Chosroes.

29.4. There chanced to be one of the men of note among the Colchians, Pharsanses by name, who had offended Gubazes and had fallen into great hatred from him, and had no courage at all to come into the king's sight.
29.5. When Phabrizus learned this, sending for Pharsanses, he conferred with him and, bringing out the whole matter, inquired of the man how he should set about the deed.

29.6. It seemed, then, to them, taking counsel in common, that Phabrizus should be in the city of Petra, and should send for Gubazes there, that he might announce to him whatever might seem to the king to be expedient for the Lazi.
29.7. But Pharsanses secretly signified to Gubazes what was being done. Therefore Gubazes by no means came to Phabrizus, but openly looked to revolt.

29.8. And Phabrizus charged the other Persians to take care of the garrison in Petra with all power and to prepare the matters of a siege most securely, but he himself with the three hundred withdrew home unsuccessful.

29.9. And Gubazes, referring to the Emperor Justinian their present situation, begged him to be forgiving of what the Lazi had formerly done, and to defend them with all power, as they wished to be rid of the rule of the Medes. For the Colchians by themselves would not be able to repel the power of the Persians.
29.10. When the Emperor Justinian heard this, he was overjoyed and sent seven thousand men and Dagisthaeus as commander, and a thousand Tzani, to the aid of the Lazi.
29.11. And these, coming to the land of Colchis, together with the Lazi and Gubazes, encamping about the wall of Petra, undertook a siege.
29.12. And the Persians there defending themselves most vigorously from the wall, much time was spent in the siege, since the Persians had chanced to store provisions enough for themselves.

29.13. Disturbed by these things, Chosroes sent against them a great army of horse and foot, over whom he set Mermeroes as commander. When Gubazes perceived this, taking counsel in common with Dagisthaeus, he did as follows.

29.14. The Boas river issues very near the borders of Tzanica in Armenia, where they dwell about the Pharangium. And at first it flows for a great extent on the right, going small and becoming crossable for all with no trouble, up to a place where on the right are the borders of the Iberians, and over against it the Caucasus mountain ends.
29.15. There many other nations dwell, both Alani and Abasgi, Christians and friends of the Romans from of old, and Zechi, and after them Huns,

29.16. who are called Sabiri. And when this river comes to where the borders of the Caucasus and Iberia are, there, other waters coming to it, it becomes far greater, and is called Phasis instead of Boas from there, having become navigable as far as the so-called Euxine Sea, where its outlets chance to be, and on either side of it is Lazica.
29.17. But on the right the whole country for a great extent is inhabited by the men there as far as the borders of Iberia.

29.18. For the villages of the Lazi are all within the river there, and towns have been made for them there from of old, among which Archaeopolis, being most strong, and there are Sebastopolis and the fortress of Pityus, and Scanda and Sarapanis by the borders of Iberia. The most notable cities there, however, are Rhodopolis and Mochiresis.

29.19. On the left of the river is the border of Lazica up to a day's journey for an unencumbered man, and the country chances to be empty of men. Bordering this country are the Romans who are called Pontic.
29.20. In the borders of Lazica, then, where men in no way dwelt, the Emperor Justinian in my time built the city of Petra.
29.21. Where John, surnamed Tzibus, establishing the monopoly, as I have said in the foregoing, became the cause of the revolt to the Lazi.

29.22. And going straight from the city of Petra toward the south wind the borders of the Romans receive one, and there are populous places there, the so-called Rhizaeum and Athenae and certain others up to the Trapezuntines.

29.23. When, then, the Lazi brought in Chosroes, crossing the Boas river and keeping the Phasis on the right, they came to Petra, in word to provide that they should not be compelled to ferry across the Phasis river with much time and toil, but in fact not wishing to display their own dwellings to the Persians.
29.24. And yet Lazica is everywhere difficult of access, both within and outside the Phasis river.
29.25. For extraordinary crags on either side of the country make very long narrows there; the Romans call such roads clisurae, hellenizing the word.
29.26. But since Lazica then chanced to be unguarded, the Persians most easily came to Petra with the leaders of the Lazi.

29.27. Now Gubazes, learning of the Persian inroad, charged Dagisthaeus to send some to guard most strongly the narrows which is outside the Phasis river, but by no means to break up the siege, until they should be able to take both Petra and the Persians there.
29.28. And he himself with the whole Colchian army came to the extremities of Lazica, to guard the narrows there with all power.

29.29. And he chanced much before to have brought the Alani and Sabiri into alliance, who had agreed for three centenaria not only to guard the land unravaged for the Lazi, but also so to make Iberia empty of men that the Persians could no longer go thence. This money Gubazes promised the emperor would give them.
29.30. He himself, then, referring to the Emperor Justinian the things agreed, besought him to send the barbarians this money and to grant some consolation to the Lazi, much afflicted.

29.31. And he said that the treasury owed him too his pay of ten years, since, being ranked among the silentiarii in the palace, he had received nothing thence from the time Chosroes came to the land of Colchis.
29.32. And the Emperor Justinian purposed to carry out the request, but some occupation coming on him, he did not send the money at the fitting time. Gubazes, then, did these things.
29.33. But Dagisthaeus (for he was a youth by no means worthy to carry through a Median war) used the present circumstances unsuitably.

29.34. For when he ought to have sent the greater part of the army to the narrows, and perhaps even himself to be present at this work, he sent only a hundred men, as though disposing of some by-task; and he himself, besieging Petra with the whole army, accomplished nothing, although the enemy were few. For at first there were not fewer than fifteen hundred,
29.35. but, by the Romans and Lazi storming the wall for a long time and being shot at and displaying valour most of all whom we know, many died, and it befell them to be reduced to very few.
29.36. The Persians, then, fallen into despair and helplessness, remained quietly, while the Romans made a trench about the wall in a small space, and the wall there at once fell.
29.37. But it befell that within this place there was a building standing no distance from the wall, which reached along the whole fallen part;
29.38. and this, becoming for the besieged instead of the wall, set them in safety no less.
29.39. Which by no means disturbed the Romans. For knowing well that, doing this same thing elsewhere, they would most easily take the city, they became much more of good hope.

29.40. Therefore Dagisthaeus declared to the emperor what had befallen, and held out that the prizes of victory should be in readiness for him, signifying with how many things it was needful for the emperor to gift both him and his brother; for they would take the Persian fortress not long after.
29.41. The Persians, then, withstood the Romans and Tzani, storming the wall most vigorously, beyond expectation, although left exceedingly few.

29.42. And when the Romans, storming the wall, accomplished nothing, they turned again to digging. And they came to such a point of this work that the foundations of the wall were no longer on the ground, but stood for the most part on emptiness, about to fall, as is likely, very soon.

29.43. And if Dagisthaeus had at once wished to set fire to the foundations, I think the city would have been taken straightway; but as it was, awaiting the hopes from the emperor and ever delaying and spending the time, he remained quietly. So these things were being done in the Roman camp here.

30.1. But Mermeroes, when he had passed the borders of Iberia with the whole army of the Medes, went forward, keeping the Phasis river on the right; for he by no means wished to go through the places of Lazica, lest some hindrance there should meet him.
30.2. For he was eager to save the city of Petra and the Persians there, although a part of the wall had fallen suddenly.
30.3. For it was suspended, as I have said; and men of the Roman army to the number of fifty, going of their own will into the city, cried out for the Emperor Justinian as gloriously victorious.
30.4. And there led them a certain young man, Armenian by race, John by name, son of Thomas, whom they called by the surname Gouzes.
30.5. This Thomas built many of the strongholds about Lazica, the emperor having charged him, and commanded the soldiers there, and seemed prudent to the emperor.
30.6. John, then, when the Persians came to blows with them, being struck, at once withdrew with his followers to the camp, since no other of the Roman army came to defend him;

30.7. but a Persian man, Mirranes by name, who commanded the garrison in Petra, fearing for the city, charged all the Persians to keep guard most exactly, and himself, sent to Dagisthaeus, held out flattering and deceitful words, agreeing with no trouble to hand over the city not long after. And by this he was able to get round him, so that the city was not at once entered by the Roman army.

30.8. And those under Mermeroes, when they came to the narrows, there the Roman garrison, being a hundred, met them, and defended themselves vigorously, and checked those who made trial of the entrance.
30.9. But the Persians by no means withdrew, but, others ever receiving those who were killed, went forward, forcing the entrance with all might.
30.10. There die of the Persians more than a thousand, and the Romans, killing, gave up, and, the throng forcing them, withdrew and, running up to the heights of the mountains there, were saved.
30.11. When Dagisthaeus learned this, he at once broke up the siege, charging the army nothing, and drove to the Phasis river; and all the Romans followed, leaving their own things in the camp.
30.12. And the Persians, seeing what was being done, opened the gates and, coming out, went to the huts of the enemy, as though to take the camp.
30.13. But the Tzani (for they had not chanced to follow Dagisthaeus) came to the rescue there at a run, and routing the enemy with no trouble killed many.

30.14. The Persians, then, fleeing, got within the wall, but the Tzani, having plundered the Roman camp, went straight to Rhizaeum. And thence, coming to Athenae, through the Trapezuntines they were conveyed home.

30.15. And Mermeroes and the army of the Medes came there on the ninth day after the retreat of Dagisthaeus; where they found left of the Persian garrison, wounded and become unfit for fighting, three hundred and fifty, and unharmed a hundred and fifty only; for all the rest had died.

30.16. Of whom the survivors had by no means thrown the bodies outside the wall, but, choking with the foulness of the smell, held out beyond expectation, that they might give the enemy no eagerness for besieging, since most of them had perished.

30.17. And Mermeroes, mocking, said that the state of the Romans was worthy of tears and lamentations, for whom affairs had come to such a point of weakness that they had been unable by any device to take a hundred and fifty Persians without walls.

30.18. And he was eager to rebuild as much of the wall as had fallen; but since he had neither lime for the moment nor any other of the things suitable for building in readiness, he devised the following.

30.19. Filling linen sacks, in which the Persians had brought provisions for themselves to the land of Colchis, with sand, he set them in the place of the stones, which, being thrown there, became instead of the wall.

30.20. And choosing out three thousand of the warlike he left them there, for whom he stored provisions not for a length of time, charging them to take care of the building of the wall; and he himself with all the rest of the army rode back.

30.21. And since on the road as he went thence he had no provision of necessaries, having left in Petra all that the army chanced to be bringing from Iberia, he purposed to go by some other journey through the mountains there, where he learned men dwelt,

30.22. that they might be able to live by plunder. On this journey one of the men of note among the Lazi, Phubelis by name, ambushed the Persians as they bivouacked, bringing with him Dagisthaeus and two thousand Romans, who killed by a raid some of the Persians pasturing horses, and plundering horses made their withdrawal in a short time. Thus Mermeroes went thence with the army of the Medes.

30.23. And Gubazes, learning what had befallen the Romans both in Petra and in the narrows, was not even so afraid, nor did he leave the guard in the narrows over against him, thinking the head of their hope was there.

30.24. For he knew well that, even if the Persians, having forced the Romans outside the Phasis river to cross the narrows and to get to Petra, were able, they would from thence fasten no harm on the country of the Lazi, having no device to cross the Phasis, especially as no ships were present to them.
30.25. For this river has depth, if any other, most sufficiently, and extends in breadth for a great extent.

30.26. And its current has such force that, casting itself into the sea, it goes for a very long way by itself, in no way mingling there. And indeed drinkable water is at hand for those sailing there to draw in the midst of the open sea.
30.27. And the Lazi have made guard-posts within the river everywhere, that the enemy, even ferrying with ships, may have no landing onto the land.
30.28. And the Emperor Justinian sent to the nation of the Sabiri the money agreed, and gifted Gubazes and the Lazi with other money.

30.29. And he chanced much before to have sent another considerable army to Lazica, who had not yet arrived there. Rhecithancus from Thrace led them, a man intelligent and good in war. So these things stood thus.

30.30. And Mermeroes, having come into the mountains, as I have said, was eager to fill Petra thence with provisions. For he thought the provisions which they had chanced to bring in with them would by no means suffice the garrison there, being three thousand.

30.31. But since what came to their hands barely sufficed for the expense of this army, being not fewer than thirty thousand, and from this they were not able to send anything worth account to Petra, reckoning, he found it better for them that the greater part of the army should depart from the land of Colchis, but that some few should remain there, who were to bring much of the provisions they should meet into the garrison in Petra, and to use the rest themselves sufficiently;
30.32. choosing out, then, about five thousand men, he left them there, and set over them three other commanders and Phabrizus.

30.33. For it seemed not necessary to him to leave more there, no enemy being anywhere about. And he himself with the rest of the army, coming to Persarmenia, remained quietly in the places about Doubios.
30.34. And the five thousand, when they came nearer the extremities of Lazica, all encamped by the Phasis river, and thence, going about in small bands, plundered the places there.
30.35. When Gubazes perceived this, he charged Dagisthaeus to come to the rescue there with haste; for the enemy would be able to do them some great harm.
30.36. And he did accordingly, and went forward with the whole Roman army, keeping the Phasis river on the left, until he came to a place where the Lazi were encamped on the other bank of the river.

30.37. And there the Phasis chanced to be crossable, which the Romans and Persians, through inexperience of the places there, by no means suspected, but the Lazi, knowing it, crossed there suddenly and mingled with the Roman army; and the Persians, choosing out a thousand of the notable among them, sent them, lest anyone should go to do mischief to the camp.
30.38. Of whom two, going first on a reconnaissance and beyond expectation falling among the enemy, reported the whole matter.

30.39. Therefore the Romans and Lazi fell suddenly upon the thousand, and none of them was able to escape, but the most were destroyed, and some of them they took alive, by whom those under Gubazes and Dagisthaeus were able to learn both the measure of the army of the Medes and the length of the road, and how their present circumstances stood.
30.40. Setting out, then, with the whole army, they went against them, reckoning so that they might fall upon them far on in the night; and they were fourteen thousand.
30.41. The Persians, then, having nothing hostile in mind, slept a long sleep; for they thought the river uncrossable, and that the thousand, no one having met them,

30.42. were going somewhere very far by the road. But the Romans and Lazi, falling unexpectedly upon them at deep dawn, found some still taking sleep, and some just roused from sleep and lying naked on their bedding.

30.43. Therefore it befell none of them to look to defence, but the most, being overtaken, died, and some the enemy took alive, among whom it chanced was one of the commanders, and a few, escaping in the dark, were saved.
30.44. And the Romans and Lazi take the camp and all the standards, and plundered many arms and great wealth, and a great quantity of horses and mules.
30.45. And making the pursuit for a very long way, they came far into Iberia. There too, meeting some other Persians, they killed many.

30.46. Thus the Persians departed from Lazica, and the Romans and Lazi, finding there the rest of the provisions and a very great quantity of flour, burned all that the barbarians had brought from Iberia to bring into Petra.

30.47. And they left many of the Lazi in the narrows, that the provisions might no longer be able to be brought in to the Persians in Petra, and with the rest of the booty and the captives they turned back.
30.48. And the fourth year was ending of the Romans' armistice with the Persians, in the twenty-third year of the Emperor Justinian holding the supreme rule.
30.49. And John the Cappadocian had come summoned by the emperor to Byzantium a year before. For at that time there came upon Theodora the empress the day that ends life.
30.50. He recovered, however, none at all of his former dignities, but on his unwilling honour remained a priest; and yet a phantom had often come to the man that he would attain the kingship.
30.51. For the demon, which is wont to glamour men, loves to hang from greater and loftier hopes those whose mind chances not to stand on a firm nature.
30.52. And to this John, then, wonder-telling visions ever foretold many other things, and that he must put on the garb of Augustus.
30.53. Now there was a certain priest in Byzantium, Augustus by name, who had the guard of the treasures of the church of Sophia.

30.54. When, then, John, having had his hair shorn, was thought worthy of the priesthood by force—for he had no garment befitting a priest—from this Augustus, being near at hand, he was compelled by those set over the work to put on the chasuble and the tunic, and to this, I think, the prophecy was for him fulfilled.
